title: Simple machines: how a small push moves a big load

summary.text: A light child can lift a heavy grown-up on a see-saw, just by sitting further from the middle. A see-saw is a lever, one of the simple machines. The six simple machines are the lever, the inclined plane (a ramp), the wheel and axle, the pulley, the wedge and the screw. Each one makes a push or a pull easier, for example by letting a small force move a heavy load. But no machine gives something for nothing: a smaller push always has to travel a longer way. The same lever rule works in your elbow, inside your muscles, and between the Earth and the Moon.
summary.art: A child sitting at the far end of a see-saw, holding a grown-up up in the air who sits close to the middle, with faint drawings of a ramp, a wheel and a bottle opener.

intro.hook: Can you lift a grown-up off the ground, using only a plank? Most children think they are far too light. On a see-saw, a light child can do it, if she sits in the right place. Where is that place, and why does it work?
intro.text: About 2,200 years ago, a Greek thinker called Archimedes worked out the rule of the lever. A lever is a long, stiff bar that turns on one point. A later writer, Pappus, says Archimedes boasted: 'Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth.' Was he showing off? Or was he right? By the end of this unit, you can decide.
intro.art: Archimedes in a Greek robe standing on a rock in space, pushing down on an impossibly long bar, the other end under the Earth.

outcomes: I can say what a simple machine is, and name the six kinds: lever, inclined plane, wheel and axle, pulley, wedge and screw.
I can find the fulcrum, the load and the effort on a lever, and spot levers at home and in my own body.
I can balance a see-saw or a ruler, and explain that weight further from the fulcrum turns more. A light thing far out can balance a heavy thing close in.
I can explain how an inclined plane, or ramp, lets me raise a load with a smaller push, by going a longer way. I can explain that a wedge and a screw are inclined planes too.
I can explain how wheels help: rolling instead of dragging, and a big wheel on a thin axle that turns a small push into a strong twist.
I can run a fair test with a ruler lever or a ramp, record my results in a table and a bar chart, and say what I think, what I saw and why.

I can explain that machines never give something for nothing: a smaller push means a longer distance. I can also give big examples of the lever rule: my arm, tiny levers in my muscles, and the Earth and the Moon balancing round one point.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces make things start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn or change shape.
terms.example: You pull a door open. You push a swing.
terms.art: A child pushing a swing and pulling a door, with arrows.

terms.meaning: Anything that makes a push or a pull easier to do. A machine can let a small force move a heavy load, change the direction of a force, or make something move further and faster. It does not need a motor.
terms.example: A spoon used to open a tin lid is a machine. So is a bicycle.
terms.art: A spoon prying open a tin lid next to a bicycle.

terms.meaning: A machine with very few parts. There are six kinds: the lever, the inclined plane, the wheel and axle, the pulley, the wedge and the screw.
terms.example: A see-saw, a slide and a doorknob are all simple machines.
terms.art: Six small icons: lever, ramp, wheel and axle, wedge, screw and pulley.

terms.meaning: The thing a machine moves or lifts.
terms.example: On a bottle opener, the load is the bottle cap.
terms.art: A bottle opener lifting a cap, the cap glowing.

terms.meaning: The force you put into a machine: your push or your pull.
terms.example: Your hand pressing down on the handle of a bottle opener.
terms.art: A hand pressing the end of a bottle opener, with an arrow.

terms.meaning: A stiff bar that turns on one point, called the fulcrum. You push on one part of the bar, and another part moves the load.
terms.example: A see-saw, a spoon opening a tin, and a hand pump are levers.
terms.art: A long bar resting on a small triangle, a box at one end and a hand at the other.

terms.meaning: The point a lever turns on. It is also called the pivot.
terms.example: The middle post of a see-saw is its fulcrum. The screw in a pair of scissors is a fulcrum.
terms.art: A see-saw with its middle post circled.

terms.meaning: A long plank with a fulcrum in the middle. One side goes up when the other goes down. It is a lever.
terms.example: The see-saw in the park.
terms.art: Two children on a park see-saw, one up, one down.

terms.meaning: When the turning effect on one side of a fulcrum is just as strong as on the other side, so nothing tips.
terms.example: A sabzi seller's weighing scale balances when the vegetables weigh the same as the weights.
terms.art: A two-pan tarazu scale level, tomatoes on one pan and a weight on the other.

terms.meaning: How strongly a force makes something turn round a fulcrum. It depends on how big the force is and how far it is from the fulcrum. Older children call it a moment, or torque.
terms.example: Pushing a door near its handle turns it easily. Pushing near the hinge hardly turns it at all.
terms.art: A door seen from above, a big arrow at the handle and a tiny effect at the hinge.

terms.meaning: A flat, sloping surface that joins a low place to a high place. Its everyday name is a ramp. Pushing a load up a long ramp takes less force than lifting it straight up.
terms.example: The slope at a railway station for trolleys and wheelchairs.
terms.art: A wheelchair rolling up a gentle ramp beside a few steps.

terms.meaning: A round disc that turns on its middle.
terms.example: Bicycle wheels, the wheels of a bullock cart, and a potter's wheel.
terms.art: A wooden bullock-cart wheel with spokes.

terms.meaning: The rod through the middle of a wheel. The wheel turns round it, or turns with it.
terms.example: A toy car's wheels are joined by thin metal axles.
terms.art: A toy car turned upside down, the axles glowing.

terms.meaning: A big wheel or handle fixed to a thin rod, the axle, so that they turn together. A small push on the big wheel makes a strong twist on the thin axle.
terms.example: A doorknob, a tap handle, a screwdriver handle and the winding handle of a well.
terms.art: A tap with its wide handle and thin spindle, a small hand arrow and a big twist arrow.

terms.meaning: A round thing put under a heavy load so the load rolls instead of sliding.
terms.example: Round logs under a boat being pulled up a beach.
terms.art: Fishermen rolling a boat up the sand on logs.

terms.meaning: A piece of hard material that narrows to a thin edge, like two inclined planes back to back. When the thin edge is pushed in, its sloping sides push things apart sideways.
terms.example: A knife, an axe and your front teeth are wedges.
terms.art: An axe splitting a log, with two ramp shapes drawn on the blade.

terms.meaning: An inclined plane wrapped round a rod. The spiral ridge is called the thread. Each turn moves the screw forward only a little, so a small twist gives a strong push.
terms.example: A wood screw goes into a plank as you turn it. A jar lid has a thread inside, and the jar has one outside.
terms.art: A paper triangle being wrapped round a pencil to make a spiral.

terms.meaning: A wheel with a groove, and a rope running over it. Pulling down on one end of the rope lifts the load on the other end. A single pulley changes the direction of your pull, not its size. You will meet pulleys properly in Class 4.
terms.example: The wheel above a village well, used to pull up the bucket. The rope that raises a flag on a flagpole.
terms.art: A well with a pulley wheel and a rope lifting a bucket.

terms.meaning: In science, work means a force moving something through a distance. You find it by multiplying the push by the distance moved. A machine can make the push smaller, but then the distance gets longer.
terms.example: Carrying a bag up a long ramp takes a small push for a long way. Lifting it straight up takes a big push for a short way.
terms.art: Two pictures: a big arrow over a short distance, and a small arrow over a long distance.

terms.meaning: What it takes to make something move, warm up or change. Energy never appears from nowhere and never disappears. It only changes from one kind into another.
terms.example: Food gives your muscles energy. Your muscles give it to the see-saw.
terms.art: A child eating a banana, then pushing down on a see-saw, with a little energy spark travelling along.

terms.meaning: The one point where a thing balances, as if all its weight were there.
terms.example: A ruler balances on your finger at its middle. A hammer balances near its heavy head.
terms.art: A ruler and a hammer each balanced on a fingertip.

terms.meaning: When you gain one thing by giving up another.
terms.example: A ramp makes the push smaller, but you have to go a longer way.
terms.art: A two-pan scale with 'smaller push' on one side and 'longer way' on the other.

explanations.definition: A simple machine is a tool with few or no moving parts. It makes a push or a pull easier, by changing how big the force is, which way it points, or how far it moves.
explanations.description: We often think a machine must have a motor. It doesn't. A spoon prying open a tin lid is a machine. So is a plank used as a ramp. A machine can do three jobs. It can turn a small force into a bigger one, like a bottle opener. It can change the direction of a force, like the pulley wheel over a well, where you pull down to lift the bucket up. Or it can make something move further and faster than your hand, like a broom. Some machines do two of these at once. Big machines, like bicycles and cranes, are many simple machines joined together.
examples: A bottle opener turns a small push on its handle into a big pull on the cap.
A pulley over a well lets you pull down to lift the bucket up.
A bicycle has levers (the brakes), wheels and axles (the wheels and pedals) and a chain.
explanations.art: A spoon opening a tin, a well pulley and a bicycle, each with arrows showing push in and push out.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a simple machine is, and what it does for us.

explanations.concept: The lever: fulcrum, load and effort
explanations.definition: A lever is a stiff bar that turns on a point called the fulcrum. You give a push, the effort, at one place. The lever moves the load at another place.
explanations.description: Think of a spoon opening a tin of ghee. The rim of the tin is the fulcrum. The lid is the load. Your hand on the far end of the spoon is the effort. Your hand moves a long way down. The tip of the spoon moves only a tiny way up. But it pushes up much harder than you pushed down. That is the lever's trick. The further your hand is from the fulcrum, compared with the lid, the harder the spoon pushes on the lid.
examples: A spoon prying a lid off a tin.
A hand pump on a village borewell. You push the long handle down, and the short end lifts the water rod.
A crowbar lifting a heavy stone.
explanations.art: A spoon opening a tin lid, with labels: fulcrum at the rim, load at the lid, effort at the hand.
explanations.context: Levers are the most common simple machine. This card names their three parts: fulcrum, load and effort.

explanations.definition: A see-saw or lever balances when the weight on one side, times its distance from the fulcrum, equals the weight on the other side, times its distance.
explanations.description: On a see-saw, the heavier person does not always go down. Distance matters too. A weight far from the fulcrum turns the plank more than the same weight close in. So a child can balance a grown-up who is twice as heavy, by sitting twice as far from the middle. Look at the chart. Two coins sit 5 cm from the pencil, and 2 times 5 is 10. One coin sits 10 cm away, and 1 times 10 is 10. Both sides make 10, so the ruler balances. Archimedes wrote this rule down about 2,200 years ago.
examples: A heavy grown-up sits close to the middle of a see-saw. A small child sits at the far end. They balance.
A sabzi seller's tarazu has two pans the same distance from the middle. So it balances when both pans weigh the same.
One coin 10 cm from a pencil balances two coins 5 cm from it.
explanations.art: A see-saw with a big grown-up close to the middle and a small child at the far end, perfectly level.
explanations.context: On a see-saw, does the heavier person always go down? This card explains the real rule, with a ruler and some coins.

chart.y: Coins times distance from the pencil
chart.note: Both sides make 10, so the ruler balances.

explanations.concept: No free gifts: a smaller push goes a longer way
explanations.definition: A machine can make a push smaller, but then the push must travel a longer distance. Push times distance stays the same, or a little more because of friction.
explanations.description: Here is the deepest idea in this unit. Machines never give you something for nothing. When a spoon lifts a tin lid, your hand moves far, and the lid moves only a little. When you walk up a long ramp, you push less, but you walk further. Scientists call push times distance 'work'. A machine cannot make the work smaller. It only spreads it out into a smaller push over a longer way. This is because energy is never made from nothing. Friction, the grip between touching things, always takes a little extra. So a real machine always needs a little more work than the ideal one.
examples: A long ramp: small push, long walk. Lifting straight up: big push, short distance.
A see-saw: the child at the far end moves down a long way. The grown-up near the middle rises only a little.
A hand pump: your hand moves a long way down, and the rod inside moves a short way up, with a bigger force.
explanations.art: A small arrow travelling a long curvy path and a big arrow travelling a short straight path, both reaching the same shelf.
explanations.context: Can a machine give you more than you put in? This card explains the rule that every machine must obey.

chart.note: Push times distance is always 12. 12 x 1 = 6 x 2 = 4 x 3 = 3 x 4 = 12.

explanations.definition: Levers come in three families, depending on what is in the middle: the fulcrum, the load or the effort.
explanations.description: In the first family, the fulcrum is in the middle, like a see-saw or a pair of scissors. These can make your push stronger. In the second family, the load is in the middle, like a nutcracker or a wheelbarrow. These also make your push stronger. In the third family, your effort is in the middle, like kitchen tongs or a broom. These make your push weaker at the far end, not stronger. So why use them? Because the far end moves further and faster than your hand. A broom's bristles sweep a wide curve while your lower hand moves only a little. Older children call these first-class, second-class and third-class levers.
examples: Fulcrum in the middle: see-saw, scissors, the handle of a hand pump.
Load in the middle: nutcracker, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, the supari cutter called a sarota.
Effort in the middle: chimta tongs, a broom, your own forearm.
explanations.art: Three rows: a see-saw, a wheelbarrow and a pair of chimta tongs, each with fulcrum, load and effort marked in three colours.
explanations.context: Not every lever looks like a see-saw. This card sorts levers into three families by what sits in the middle.

explanations.concept: The inclined plane: a gentle slope instead of a big lift
explanations.definition: An inclined plane, or ramp, is a sloping surface that joins a low place to a high place. The longer and gentler the ramp, the smaller the push needed to move a load up it.
explanations.description: Lifting a heavy box straight up onto a step takes a big push. Pushing it up a ramp takes a smaller push. But you push it a longer way. Look at the chart. A newton is the unit scientists use to measure a push or a pull. To raise a bag 1 metre, you can lift it straight up with a push of 12 newtons. Up a ramp 2 metres long, you need only about 6 newtons. Up a ramp 4 metres long, about 3. Every time, push times distance is 12. Real ramps also have friction, so the push is a bit bigger. Mountain roads that zigzag up the ghats are ramps too. Because they are long and gentle, a truck needs a smaller push from its engine to climb them.
examples: Ramps at railway stations, for wheelchairs, trolleys and suitcases.
The zigzag roads that climb the ghats to hill stations.
A plank used to roll a heavy drum up into a truck.
explanations.art: A loading plank from the ground to a truck, a worker rolling a drum up it, the truck's height marked.
explanations.context: How do you get a heavy thing onto a high place without lifting it? This card explains the ramp, with numbers.

chart.title: Push needed to move a 12-newton bag up to a 1-metre-high step (made-up, with no friction)
chart.note: Push times distance is always 12. 12 x 1 = 6 x 2 = 4 x 3 = 3 x 4 = 12.

explanations.concept: Wheels, rollers and the wheel and axle
explanations.definition: Wheels help in two ways. Rolling is much easier than dragging. And a big wheel fixed to a thin axle turns a small push on the wheel into a strong twist on the axle.
explanations.description: The first trick is rolling. A dragged box rubs along the ground the whole way. A wheel touches the ground at only one small spot, and that spot lifts off as the wheel turns. So there is far less rubbing, which scientists call friction. The second trick is the wheel and axle. Turning a tap's thin rod with bare fingers is hard. Its wide handle makes it easy. Your hand goes round a big circle. The rod turns round a small circle, but strongly. A wheel and axle is a lever that goes round and round. Doorknobs, screwdriver handles, steering wheels and the handle of a well winch all work this way.
examples: A screwdriver with a fat handle turns a tight screw more easily than one with a thin handle.
The wide handle on a well winch lifts a heavy bucket.
A bicycle's pedal cranks turn the front gear wheel.
explanations.art: A tap with and without its handle, and a well winch with its long crank, a small arrow at the crank and a big arrow at the rope.
explanations.context: Wheels are everywhere. This card explains the two different jobs a wheel can do.

explanations.concept: Wedges and screws: inclined planes in disguise
explanations.definition: A wedge is two inclined planes back to back. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped round a rod.
explanations.description: When an axe hits a log, its thin edge goes in a little. Its sloping sides push the two halves of the wood apart sideways, with a much bigger force than the blow. A screw is a long ramp wound round and round a rod. Turning it many times moves it in only a little, but very strongly. That is the trade-off again: a small push over a long way. You can see it for yourself. Cut a triangle from paper, with one square corner. Lay its shortest side along a pencil, and roll the paper round the pencil. The sloping edge winds round in a spiral, just like a screw thread.
examples: A knife, an axe and a nail's point are wedges.
Your front teeth are wedges, for biting. Your back teeth are flatter, for grinding.
A wood screw, a jar lid and a bottle top have screw threads.
explanations.art: A paper triangle wrapped round a pencil to make a spiral, next to a real screw.
explanations.context: This card shows that two other simple machines, wedges and screws, are really ramps in disguise. You will meet them again in Class 4.

explanations.concept: Your body is full of levers
explanations.definition: Your bones are levers. Your joints are their fulcrums. Your muscles give the effort.
explanations.description: Bend your arm with a water bottle in your hand. Your elbow is the fulcrum. Your biceps, the muscle at the front of your upper arm, pulls on your forearm very close to the elbow. In a grown-up, that is about 5 cm from the elbow. Your hand holds the bottle about 35 cm away. 35 divided by 5 is 7. So the muscle must pull about 7 times as hard as the bottle's weight. Why would a body be built so badly? It isn't bad. It is a trade-off. Because the muscle is close to the fulcrum, your hand moves 7 times as far and as fast as the muscle shortens. That lets you throw, wave and catch. Standing on tiptoe uses your foot as a lever with the load in the middle. Your jaw is a lever too. Its fulcrum is the joint just in front of your ear.
examples: Your forearm, with the elbow as fulcrum: effort in the middle, for speed.
Standing on tiptoe: the ball of your foot is the fulcrum, and your calf muscle lifts your whole weight.
Nodding your head: the joint at the top of your spine is the fulcrum. Your head rocks on it like a see-saw.
explanations.art: An arm holding a water bottle, the elbow marked as the fulcrum, the biceps pulling near it, and the hand far out, with 5 cm and 35 cm marked.
explanations.context: You carry levers with you everywhere. This card shows where they are in your own body, and why they are built for speed.

explanations.definition: Inside every muscle are billions of tiny molecules called myosin. Each one has a small arm that swings like a lever, pulling on a thread and making the muscle shorter.
explanations.description: In 1954, two teams found out how muscles shorten. Hugh Huxley and Jean Hanson were one team. Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke were the other. Muscles are made of two kinds of thin threads that slide past each other. Later, scientists found what does the pulling. Myosin is a tiny molecule with a head and a stiff neck. The head grabs the other kind of thread. A small change near the head is made bigger by the stiff neck, which swings like a lever. In 1993, Ivan Rayment and his team first saw the shape of a myosin head and its lever arm. Each swing moves the thread only a few millionths of a millimetre. But billions of swings together lift your arm. So the lever rule works far below what any eye can see. Scientists still study exactly how each step is timed.
examples: Every time you blink, millions of myosin levers swing.
Your heart beats because myosin levers in its muscle pull, again and again, all your life.
explanations.art: A zoom from an arm to a muscle to threads sliding past each other, with tiny myosin heads grabbing a thread and their necks swinging like oars.
explanations.context: Levers are not only big. This card zooms into a muscle to find levers made of single molecules.

explanations.concept: The Earth and the Moon on a see-saw
explanations.definition: The Earth and the Moon both swing round one shared balance point. Like a see-saw, the balance point sits much closer to the heavier one, the Earth.
explanations.description: We say the Moon goes round the Earth. That is nearly true, but not quite. Imagine the Earth and Moon on the ends of a giant, invisible see-saw. The Earth is about 81 times heavier than the Moon. So the balance point must be about 81 times closer to the Earth's centre than to the Moon's. That puts it about 4,700 kilometres from the Earth's centre. The Earth is about 6,400 kilometres from its centre to its surface. So the balance point is inside the Earth, about 1,700 kilometres under our feet. Every month the Earth wobbles round it. The Sun and Jupiter have a balance point too. It sits just outside the Sun's surface. In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz saw a far-away star wobbling like this. The wobble showed a planet was going round it. It was the first planet found going round a star like our Sun. They shared a Nobel Prize in 2019. Thousands of planets have been found since, many of them by their star's wobble.
examples: Hold hands with a grown-up and spin round together. You both turn round a point nearer the grown-up.
Astronomers find planets round other stars by watching the stars wobble.
explanations.art: The Earth and the Moon on the ends of a cosmic see-saw, its balance point drawn inside the Earth, a dotted circle showing the Earth's wobble.
explanations.context: The see-saw rule works in space too. This card shows the balance point of the Earth and the Moon, and how it helps astronomers find new planets.

explanations.concept: Who first used levers, ramps and wheels?
explanations.description: Nobody knows who first used a lever. It was long before anyone wrote things down. Different people get the credit in different stories. Here are the main ones.
examples: The shaduf is a pole on a post with a bucket at one end and a heavy stone at the other. People in Mesopotamia and Egypt used it to lift water, about 4,000 years ago.
Clay toy carts with wheels have been found at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, cities of the Indus Valley, about 4,500 years old.
One of the oldest wooden wheels ever found, from a marsh near Ljubljana in Slovenia, is about 5,100 years old.

perspectives.who: Archimedes, a Greek thinker in Syracuse, who lived about 2,200 years ago
perspectives.explanation: He did not invent the lever. But he was the first we know of to prove its rule with geometry: weight times distance must match on both sides.

perspectives.who: Thinkers in China called the Mohists, writing at about the same time
perspectives.explanation: Their writings also describe how a balance arm tips when a weight is moved further out. Their work is much less famous in Western books.

perspectives.who: Al-Jazari, an engineer in what is now Turkey, who finished his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices in 1206
perspectives.explanation: He drew and explained dozens of machines: water-lifting machines with wheels, cranks and levers, and clocks with moving figures. One of his water pumps turned round-and-round movement into back-and-forth movement, an idea still used in many machines today. His name is missing from many textbooks.

perspectives.who: Farmers, builders and women working at home, whose names were never written down
perspectives.explanation: They used levers, ramps and rollers for thousands of years before anyone wrote rules. In India, the dhenki rice pounder and the well lever called the picottah or etram are two examples. The dhenki was worked mostly by women.

explanations.art: A timeline strip: a farmer at a shaduf, an Indus Valley clay toy cart, Archimedes drawing in the sand, and a woman working a dhenki.
explanations.context: This card asks who should get the credit for levers and wheels. The answer is less simple than most books say.

explanations.concept: How were giant stones raised long ago?
explanations.description: People built pyramids, temples and forts with stones far too heavy to lift by hand. They had no engines. Most experts agree they used ramps, levers, sledges and rollers, and very many workers. But exactly how they did it is still argued about.
examples: The Great Pyramid in Egypt has more than two million stone blocks.
The tower of the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur, about 1,000 years old, is about 66 metres tall. It is topped by a huge capstone.

perspectives.explanation: Long ramps of earth and mud brick were built up beside the pyramid, and the stones were dragged up on sledges. In 2018, a team from France and Britain found a steep ramp with stairs and posts at an old quarry in Egypt, called Hatnub. Ropes may have run round the posts, like a simple pulley.

perspectives.who: Jean-Pierre Houdin, a French architect, and others
perspectives.explanation: A ramp may have spiralled up inside the pyramid itself. Many archaeologists are not convinced.
The capstone was dragged up a very long earth ramp, starting from a village several kilometres away. Historians are not sure the story is true, or whether the capstone is one stone or several.

explanations.art: Workers dragging a stone block on a sledge up a long mud-brick ramp beside a half-built pyramid, with posts and ropes on the ramp.
explanations.context: Long before engines, people raised giant stones. This card is about how they may have done it with ramps and levers, and what is still unknown.

agreed.text: A lever balances when weight times distance from the fulcrum is the same on both sides.
agreed.evidence: Archimedes proved it about 2,200 years ago. Anyone can test it with a ruler, a pencil and some coins, and it works every time.

chart.y: Coins times distance from the pencil
chart.note: Both sides make 10, so the ruler balances.

agreed.text: Machines can make a push smaller or change its direction, but they never give out more work than you put in.
agreed.evidence: Every careful measurement of a lever, ramp or pulley shows it. A smaller push always goes a longer way. Nobody has ever built a machine that keeps going by itself for ever.

agreed.text: A longer, gentler ramp needs a smaller push to raise a load to the same height.
agreed.evidence: Pull a loaded toy truck up ramps of different lengths with a rubber band or a forcemeter. The longer ramp needs less pull.

chart.title: Made-up example results: rubber band stretch when pulling a loaded toy truck up to the same height
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different. A longer stretch means a bigger pull.

agreed.text: Rolling a load on wheels or rollers takes much less push than dragging it.
agreed.evidence: Builders have used rollers and wheels for thousands of years. A forcemeter, a spring tool that measures pulls, shows the difference straight away.

agreed.text: Your bones and muscles work as levers, with your joints as fulcrums.
agreed.evidence: Doctors and scientists have measured where muscles join the bones, using X-rays and careful study of bodies. The lever rule predicts how hard each muscle must pull.

challenging.claim: On a see-saw, the heavier person always goes down.
challenging.who: Most of us, before we try it
challenging.for: If two people sit at the very ends, the heavier one does go down.
challenging.against: Distance from the fulcrum matters as much as weight. A heavy grown-up who slides close to the middle can be lifted by a small child at the far end.
challenging.context: This card looks at a very common idea about see-saws, and why it is only half right.

challenging.who: A common way of talking about machines
challenging.for: A machine really does make a job feel easier. You need a smaller push.
challenging.against: In science, work means push times distance. A machine makes the push smaller but the distance longer, so the work stays the same. Friction even adds a little. Machines make jobs easier, not smaller.
challenging.context: People often say machines save work. This card asks whether that is true in the scientist's sense of the word.

challenging.claim: A clever enough wheel could keep turning for ever by itself, giving free energy.
challenging.who: Bhaskara II, a great Indian mathematician, described such a wheel in about 1150. Many inventors in Europe and elsewhere tried for centuries after him.
challenging.for: His wheel carried mercury, a heavy liquid metal, sealed inside tubes. The idea was that the mercury would always make one side heavier, so the wheel would keep turning.
challenging.against: No such wheel has ever worked. The weights shift, but the turning effects on both sides always end up balanced, and friction slowly stops the wheel. Energy cannot come from nothing. Bhaskara II was a brilliant mathematician, and this one idea did not work. Even great thinkers can be wrong.
challenging.context: For hundreds of years, people dreamed of a machine that never stops. This card is about one of the oldest designs, from India.

challenging.who: Many popular books and quiz shows
challenging.for: Archimedes wrote down the law of the lever, and proved it. He is famous for it.
challenging.against: Farmers were lifting water with levers like the shaduf almost 2,000 years before he was born. Archimedes explained the lever. People whose names nobody wrote down invented it and used it.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for the lever.

challenging.claim: The peoples of ancient Mexico never knew about the wheel.
challenging.for: The Aztecs, the Maya and their neighbours did not use carts or wagons.
challenging.against: Archaeologists have found little clay animal toys on wheels in Mexico, many centuries old. So they knew the wheel. Why they did not use it for carts is still debated. They had no horses or oxen to pull carts. Their land had many jungles and steep mountains.
challenging.context: This card is about the wheel in the Americas, and how a 'missing' invention can be a choice.

challenging.claim: With a long enough lever, Archimedes really could have moved the Earth.
challenging.who: A boast that the writer Pappus says Archimedes made
challenging.for: The lever rule has no limit. In theory, a long enough lever turns any small push into any big push.
challenging.against: The lever would have to be unimaginably long, and much stiffer than any material. He would need a place to stand outside the Earth. And to lift the Earth by even 1 centimetre, his hand would have to travel so far that it would take longer than the age of the universe. The rule is right, but the job is impossible.
challenging.context: Archimedes is said to have boasted: 'Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth.' This card asks whether he could have done it.

big_questions.q: Is there any machine that gives you something for nothing?
big_questions.hint: Every time a machine makes your push smaller, what gets bigger?

big_questions.q: Why is your biceps joined so close to your elbow, when that makes it work harder?
big_questions.hint: Watch how far your hand moves when your muscle shortens just a little.

big_questions.q: Could the same rule that balances a see-saw in the park also work for planets and stars?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Earth and the Moon sitting on the two ends of a see-saw.

big_questions.q: The Moon does not simply go round the Earth. Both swing round a shared balance point. Is anything in space really standing still while other things go round it?
big_questions.hint: Think of spinning round while holding hands with a grown-up. Which of you stays still?

big_questions.q: Ramps help people in wheelchairs, parents with prams and grandparents with sore knees. Who decides whether a building has a ramp, and who is left out when it doesn't?
big_questions.hint: Look at the steps of a shop, a temple or a school near you. Could everyone get in?

big_questions.q: Archimedes gets the credit for the lever, but farmers used levers long before him. Who should get the credit: the person who uses an idea, or the person who writes it down?
big_questions.hint: Think of a recipe your family makes that nobody ever wrote down.

big_questions.q: A machine trades a small push for a long distance. When would you rather push harder for a shorter way?
big_questions.hint: Think of carrying a light bag to a high shelf. Would you lift it straight up, or walk up a long ramp?

big_questions.q: If you had a lever long enough, what would you want to move, and where would you stand?
big_questions.hint: Remember Archimedes' boast about moving the Earth.

big_questions.q: Your muscles are moved by billions of tiny molecules that swing like levers. Are you a machine?
big_questions.hint: What can you do that a see-saw can't? What can a machine do that you can't?

big_questions.q: The peoples of ancient Mexico made toys with wheels but never built carts. Is a better tool always the best choice?
big_questions.hint: What would a cart need to be useful: roads, animals, flat land?

big_questions.q: Why does a little push far from a door's hinge open it more easily than a big push close to the hinge?
big_questions.hint: Try it. Where does the door turn from?

story.title: Where Jonaki Stood
story.note: The dhenki is a real foot-worked rice pounder, used in Assam, Bengal, Odisha and beyond, and mostly worked by women. Magh Bihu, the feast night of Uruka and pitha rice cakes are real. Jonaki, Bubu, Pehi and what happened to them are made up.
text: In a village in Assam, at the edge of the rice fields, the dhenki lived in a shed of its own. It was a long beam of jackfruit wood, as long as three children lying head to toe. It rested on a short wooden post, nearer one end than the other, so it could rock like a see-saw. From the long end hung a heavy wooden head with an iron ring on its nose. Under the head was a hollow in the floor, where the rice went. When someone stepped down hard on the short end, the head rose into the air. When they stepped off, the head fell. Thud. And the rice in the hollow turned, little by little, into flour.

Every winter, before Magh Bihu, the harvest festival, the dhenki woke up. The women of Jonaki's house soaked the new rice overnight. Then they pounded it for pitha, the sweet rice cakes of the festival, stuffed with sesame and jaggery. Jonaki's mother stepped on the beam, steady as a clock. Her aunt Pehi crouched by the hollow with a long bamboo stick. Between thuds, she pushed the rice back under the head. Thud, push. Thud, push. The whole shed smelled of wet rice and woodsmoke.

Jonaki was eight. Every year she asked to step on the dhenki, and every year Pehi laughed. She lifted Jonaki by the armpits, as if she were weighing a fish. 'Too light,' she said. 'The dhenki listens only to heavy feet.'

On the morning of Uruka, the feast night before Magh Bihu, a neighbour came running. Her cow was giving birth, and the calf was stuck. Jonaki's mother knew cows better than anyone in the village. She tied up her mekhela, the long wrapped skirt, and ran. Pehi ran after her with a bucket of warm water.
'Keep the rice covered,' her mother called over her shoulder. 'We'll be back soon.'

They were not back soon. The sun climbed over the bamboo, and then began to slide down the other side. Jonaki lifted the cloth from the basket. The soaked rice was drying at the edges. Rice that dries before it is pounded makes flour that cracks. Pitha made from it falls apart in your fingers. Tonight the whole village would eat together, and her family would bring nothing whole.

Jonaki went into the shed. Her little brother Bubu, who was five, followed her like a shadow. She tipped a handful of rice into the hollow. She climbed onto the short end of the beam and stood in the middle of it, where it felt steady and comfortable. She pressed down with all her weight.
Nothing happened. The head sat in the hollow, as heavy as a sleeping dog.

She jumped. The beam shivered, and the head lifted no more than a finger's width. Bubu laughed, and then he climbed up beside her and jumped too. The head twitched and settled. They jumped until their legs ached and Bubu started to cry.
'Too light,' Jonaki said, in Pehi's voice, and hated it.

She sat down on the cold floor with her back against the post and looked at the beam. It was dark brown all over, rubbed shiny with oil and years. Except in one place. At the very tip of the short end, the wood was worn pale, as smooth as a river stone. There was a shallow dip in it, the shape of a heel.

Jonaki looked at that dip for a long time. That was where her mother's heel went. And Pehi's. And the heels of all the women who had pounded rice in this shed, winter after winter, before Jonaki was born. Not in the steady, comfortable middle. Right at the very end, as far from the post as a foot could go.

She thought of the see-saw at school. When big Dipen sat at the far end, she shot up into the air and stayed there. But once he slid in close to the middle, to tease her, and suddenly she could push him up. She had not been any heavier that day. She had only been further away from the middle than he was.
Jonaki stood up. She stepped onto the beam and walked along it to the very end. She put her heel into the pale dip, where it fitted as if it had been waiting. She pressed down.
The head rose. Not a finger's width this time, but a whole hand's height. Then it dropped, with a small, honest thud. Some grains of rice jumped.
'Bubu,' she said. 'Come here. Not there. Here, right at the end, with me.'
Bubu climbed up and held on to her waist. His small feet squeezed into the dip beside hers. 'Now,' said Jonaki. They pressed down together.
The head swung up, up, as high as Jonaki's knee. 'Off!' They hopped back, and it fell. THUD. The whole shed shook, and the rice in the hollow leapt like popcorn.

They found the rhythm slowly. Press together, lift, hop off, thud. Jonaki jumped down after every few thuds and pushed the rice back with Pehi's long bamboo stick, never her fingers. Then she climbed back to the end. Bubu made up a song to keep time. It had only four words, and he sang them so loudly that the hens ran away.

The light went orange, then grey. When Jonaki's mother came home, with mud on her mekhela and a new calf safe behind her in the neighbour's shed, she heard the thudding from the road. She thought Pehi must have run back early. She looked into the shed.
There were two children at the far end of the dhenki, holding on to each other. Beside the hollow sat a basket, nearly full of soft white flour.
Her mother did not say anything at first. She looked at their feet, pressed into the pale dip at the very tip of the beam. Then she laughed, very quietly.
'So,' she said. 'The dhenki listens to light feet too.'
'Only if they stand in the right place,' said Jonaki.

That night, under the stars, the whole village ate together round the fires of Uruka. Jonaki's family's pitha did not crack. And in the dark shed at the edge of the fields, the pale dip at the end of the beam was very slightly deeper than it had been that morning.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Jonaki does not get heavier. She moves to the very end of the beam, as far from the fulcrum as she can. On a lever, a force far from the fulcrum turns it much more than the same force close in. So her small weight at the tip lifts the heavy head that her weight near the middle could not. When Bubu adds his weight at the same far point, the turning grows again. The pale, worn dip at the end of the beam is the record of generations of women who knew this rule long before anyone wrote it down. The story also quietly asks whose knowledge gets written down, and whose is kept in wood and habit.
ask: When Jonaki stood in the middle of the beam, nothing happened. What did she change to make the head rise?
Why do you think the wood at the very tip of the beam was worn pale?
How did remembering the see-saw at school help Jonaki?
Pehi said the dhenki listens only to heavy feet. Was she right, wrong, or half right?
Jonaki learned the rule from the women who used the dhenki before her. Who in your family knows something useful that was never written in a book?

rules: Glue the printed strip on a 30 cm ruler. Tape a round pencil to the table so it cannot roll. Lay the ruler across it, at the middle, so it can rock.
Shuffle the order cards. Start with the Level 1 cards. Move up a level when you get two right in a row.
On your turn, read a card out loud. Before you touch any coins, say your plan out loud.
Then place the coins. If it balances on your first try, you win 2 points. If it balances on your second try, you win 1 point.
Predict cards: everyone guesses first. Each player who guessed right wins 1 point.
Mystery cards: solve the mystery weight. Then check it with real coins. A right answer wins 3 points.
The first player to 15 points is the Bazaar Master.

flow.do: 1. Glue the strip onto a ruler, or write the peg numbers on it with a pen. 2. Lay a round pencil on the table and stick each end down with tape, so it cannot roll. 3. Lay the ruler across the pencil, exactly at the middle. 4. Check it balances empty. If it doesn't, slide it a little until it does.
flow.say: This ruler is a see-saw. The pencil is its fulcrum, the point it turns on. Let's check it balances when it is empty.
flow.kid: Put the ruler across a round pencil. The pencil is the fulcrum. Slide the ruler until it balances with nothing on it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Balance Bazaar. It is a see-saw puzzle game played on a ruler balanced on a pencil, with coins as weights. It is based on the Balancing Act game from PhET, a free science website.

flow.do: Play a Level 1 card together as a practice round: 2 coins on left peg 2, balance with 2 coins.
flow.say: Here's our first order. Two coins sit on peg 2 on the left. Where should we put two coins on the right?
flow.kid: First order: 2 coins on left peg 2. Where do 2 coins go on the right? Say your guess. Then try it.

ask.q: Why did the same coins need the same peg?
good: Same weight, same distance, so it's even.
Both sides turn the ruler the same amount.

check.q: Bazaar order: 2 coins wait on left peg 2. Where do you put your 2 coins to fill the order?
check.why: Peg 2 fills the order: same coins, same distance, so both sides turn the ruler equally. A player who picks peg 4 thinks further out always helps. Here it would tip the ruler to the right.

flow.do: 1. Take turns with the cards. 2. Each player says a plan before placing coins. 3. Move up to Level 2 and Level 3 as players get two right in a row.
flow.say: Now the coins on each side are different. Can fewer coins balance more coins? Where would they have to sit?
flow.kid: Take turns. Read a card. Say your plan out loud first. Can fewer coins balance more coins? Where should they sit?
flow.parent: The rule is coins times peg number must match on both sides. For example, 2 coins on peg 2 makes 2 times 2, which is 4. 1 coin on peg 4 makes 1 times 4, which is also 4. Let your child find this by trying. Only say the rule after they have spotted a pattern. The ruler will not always sit perfectly level. If it rocks, or stays up when you let go, it is balanced. If one end drops to the table and stays there, it has tipped.

ask.q: 1 coin balanced 2 coins. Where was the 1 coin?
good: Twice as far from the pencil.

flow.do: Play the Predict cards. Everyone says tip left, tip right, or balance, before you test.
flow.say: Before we test, everyone guess. Will it tip left, tip right, or balance? Let's see who was right.
flow.kid: Predict card! Guess first: tip left, tip right, or balance? Then test it.

check.q: Predict card: 2 coins on left peg 4, 4 coins on right peg 2. Place your guess token. What happens?
options: It tips left, because the left side is further out
It tips right, because there are more coins
It balances, because 2 times 4 and 4 times 2 both make 8
check.why: It balances: 2 times 4 is 8, and 4 times 2 is 8. A player who guesses 'tips right' is counting coins and forgetting distance. A player who guesses 'tips left' is counting distance and forgetting coins.

flow.do: Try one Level 4 mystery card. Use the rule to find the weight of an eraser or a key in coins.
flow.say: Now we're detectives. A tarazu weighs vegetables by balancing them against known weights. How many coins does the eraser weigh?
flow.kid: Mystery card! The eraser balances some coins. How many coins does the eraser weigh? Use the rule to find out.
flow.think: Could you weigh a pencil with this ruler and some coins? How would you do it?

flow.do: Add up the points and find the Bazaar Master.
flow.say: Who's the Bazaar Master? And what was the trick that helped you most?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Who won? What trick helped you most?

printables.title: Three sorting mats
items: RAMP, the inclined plane (and its cousins, the wedge and the screw)
WHEEL (wheels, rollers, wheel and axle, pulleys)

rules: Shuffle the object cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take a card and read it out loud. Put it on the LEVER, RAMP or WHEEL mat.
If it is a lever, point to where its fulcrum is, or act it out. That wins a bonus token.
Say what the machine trades. For example, small push for a long way. That wins another token.
If someone disagrees, talk it through. Some things are more than one machine.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the three mats. 2. Shuffle the object cards face down. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card shows a simple machine. Is it a lever, a ramp or a wheel? And where is its fulcrum, the point it turns on?
flow.kid: Lay out three mats: LEVER, RAMP and WHEEL. Mix up the cards. For each card, decide which mat it goes on.
flow.context: This is the first step of Machine Spotter. It is a card game where players sort everyday objects into levers, ramps and wheels.

flow.do: 1. Take turns drawing a card and placing it. 2. For levers, the player shows the fulcrum, with a real object if you have one. 3. Give tokens for each good reason.
flow.say: Where does this one turn? Where do you push, and where does it push back?
flow.kid: Draw a card. Put it on a mat. If it's a lever, show where it turns. Say where you push.
flow.parent: Tricky ones: scissors are two levers joined at one fulcrum. A wheelbarrow is a lever (the wheel is the fulcrum) and also has a wheel. A knife and an axe are wedges, which are ramps in disguise. A jar lid and a spiral staircase are screws, which are ramps wrapped round. A doorknob, a tap and a screwdriver are each a wheel and axle. Your forearm's fulcrum is the elbow. Your jaw's fulcrum is just in front of your ear. A cricket bat held in two hands is a lever too: the top hand is the fulcrum, and the bottom hand pushes.

ask.q: Where is the fulcrum of a nutcracker?
good: At the hinge at the end.
Where the two arms are joined.

RAMP, because its blade is two slopes back to back

items.p: What is a simple machine?
opts: A tool with few parts that makes a push or pull easier
Only very big things, like cranes
items.why: A simple machine has few parts and makes a push or pull easier. Picking 'a motor' is very common, because many machines we see have one. But a spoon opening a tin is a machine with no motor. A child who picks 'makes energy' thinks machines give out extra. They never do.

items.p: The point a lever turns on is called the ____.
items.why: The fulcrum, also called the pivot, is where a lever turns. On a see-saw it is the post in the middle.

items.p: On a bottle opener, what is the load?
items.why: The load is what you want to move: the cap. Picking 'your hand' mixes up the effort, your push, with the load.
items.art: A bottle opener on a cap.

items.p: Match each part of a see-saw to its name.
items.why: The fulcrum is where it turns. The load is what is lifted. The effort is your push.

items.p: A heavy grown-up and a light child are on a see-saw. Where should the grown-up sit to balance?
items.why: Weight close to the fulcrum turns the plank less. So the heavy grown-up moves in, and the light child stays far out. A child who picks 'never balance' thinks the heavier person always goes down. Distance matters too.
items.art: A see-saw with a grown-up and a child.

items.p: On a see-saw, the heavier person always goes down.
items.why: False. Distance from the fulcrum matters as much as weight. A heavy person close to the middle can be lifted by a light person far out.

items.p: Sort these into the right simple machine.
items.why: See-saws and scissors turn on a fulcrum, so they are levers. Slides and slopes join low places to high places, so they are ramps. Bicycle wheels and doorknobs turn round an axle, so they are wheels.

items.p: Why is a long, gentle ramp easier than a short, steep one, when both reach the same step?
opts: The long ramp needs a smaller push, but you push for longer
The long ramp makes the load lighter
The short ramp has no friction
items.why: A longer ramp spreads the job out: a smaller push over a longer way. Picking 'makes the load lighter' is a common idea. The load weighs just the same. Only the push you need changes.
items.context: A ramp is a slope that joins a low place to a high place. This question compares a long ramp and a short ramp up to the same height.

items.p: Which is easiest: dragging a heavy box, or rolling it on round pencils?
items.why: Rollers touch the floor at only a few small spots, so there is much less rubbing, or friction. A child who picks 'the same' thinks only the box's weight matters. How it touches the floor matters too.

items.p: A big handle fixed to a thin rod, like a tap or a doorknob, is called a wheel and ____.
items.why: A wheel and axle turns a small push on the big wheel into a strong twist on the thin rod.

items.p: You push a door to open it. Where is it easiest to push?
opts: Far from the hinges, near the handle
In the middle of the door, top to bottom
items.why: The hinges are where the door turns, like the fulcrum of a lever. A push far from the hinges turns the door much more. Picking 'the same everywhere' is common, because the door weighs the same. Try pushing near the hinges. It is very hard!
items.art: A door seen from above with arrows at the hinge and at the handle.

items.p: A machine must have a motor.
items.why: False. A see-saw, a ramp and a spoon are all machines with no motor.

items.p: Your arm is a lever. What is its fulcrum?
items.why: Your forearm turns at the elbow, so the elbow is the fulcrum. Picking 'your hand' mixes up the place the load is held with the place it turns.

items.p: Name three levers you can find in your home. For each one, say where its fulcrum is.
items.a: For example: scissors, fulcrum at the screw in the middle. A spoon opening a tin, fulcrum at the rim. A door, fulcrum at the hinges.
items.why: Any three real levers with the right fulcrum are correct.

items.p: Pehi says, 'The dhenki listens only to heavy feet.' Is she right? Use the word fulcrum in your answer.
items.a: She is only half right. A light person can lift the heavy head too, if they stand at the very end of the beam, far from the fulcrum. Weight far from the fulcrum turns the beam more.
items.why: A good answer says that where you stand, not only how heavy you are, matters.
items.context: In this unit's story, Jonaki is told she is too light to work the dhenki. A dhenki is a long wooden beam on a post that pounds rice when you step on one end.

items.p: Draw a see-saw with a grown-up and a child balancing it. Mark the fulcrum.
items.a: The grown-up sits close to the middle. The child sits near the end. The fulcrum is the post in the middle.
items.why: Heavy near, light far makes a balance.

items.p: Two coins sit 5 cm from the pencil on a ruler see-saw. Where must one coin go on the other side to balance them?
items.why: 2 coins times 5 cm is 10. 1 coin times 10 cm is also 10. So the one coin goes 10 cm away. Picking 5 cm means only the place is matched, not the weight. A child who picks 'can't balance' thinks fewer coins always lose.

chart.note: Both sides make 10, so the ruler balances.

items.p: 3 coins sit on peg 2. To balance them with coins on peg 3, you need ____ coins.
items.why: 3 times 2 is 6. 2 times 3 is also 6. So 2 coins on peg 3 balance 3 coins on peg 2.

items.p: Kitchen tongs (chimta) have your hand in the middle. They make your squeeze weaker at the tips. Why use them?
opts: The tips move further than your fingers, and keep your hand away from the heat
items.why: In tongs, the effort is in the middle, so they trade strength for distance. The tips open wide, and your fingers stay away from the hot pan. Picking 'stronger' is very common, because we expect every lever to make pushes bigger. Some levers are for distance and speed instead.

items.p: Sort these levers by what is in the middle.
items.why: Scissors and see-saws turn in the middle. In a nutcracker and a wheelbarrow, the load sits between the fulcrum and your hands. In tongs and a broom, your push is in the middle.

items.p: A worker rolls a heavy drum up a plank into a truck. Then she uses a longer plank to the same truck. What changes?
opts: She needs a smaller push, but rolls it further
items.why: A longer ramp to the same height is gentler, so the push is smaller. But she rolls the drum a longer way. Picking 'the drum gets lighter' is a common mix-up between weight and push.

items.p: Look at the chart. Lifting a bag straight up 1 metre takes 12 newtons. Up a 3-metre ramp, about how much push does it take, with no friction?
items.why: Push times distance stays the same: 12 times 1 is 12. So for 3 metres, the push is 12 divided by 3, which is 4 newtons. Picking 36 means multiplying instead of sharing. A longer ramp makes the push smaller, not bigger.

chart.title: Push needed to move a 12-newton bag up to a 1-metre-high step (made-up, with no friction)
chart.note: Push times distance is always 12. 12 x 1 = 6 x 2 = 4 x 3 = 3 x 4 = 12.

items.context: A newton is the unit for measuring a push or a pull. This question compares lifting a bag straight up and pushing it up ramps.

items.p: A well winch with a long handle lifts a heavy bucket more easily than turning the thin rod with your fingers.
items.why: True. The long handle is the big wheel of a wheel and axle. Your hand goes round a big circle with a small push, and the rod twists strongly.

items.p: A bicycle has many simple machines. Which part is a lever?
items.why: The brake handle turns on a fulcrum. A small squeeze of your fingers becomes a strong pull on the brake cable. A child who picks the tyre is mixing up wheels and levers. The tyre is part of a wheel.

items.p: Match each thing to the simple machine it really is.
items.why: A knife is two ramps back to back, a wedge. A jar lid is a ramp wrapped round, a screw. A doorknob is a wheel and axle.

items.p: Your biceps pulls on your forearm about 5 cm from your elbow. Your hand is about 35 cm from your elbow. How many times as hard must the muscle pull as the weight in your hand?
items.why: 35 divided by 5 is 7. The muscle is 7 times closer to the fulcrum, so it must pull about 7 times as hard. A child who picks 'about the same' thinks the muscle pulls the load straight up. But the arm is a lever, built for speed.

chart.title: Your arm as a lever (typical grown-up numbers)
rows: Where your hand holds a load
How many times further the hand is

items.context: Your arm is a lever. The elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps muscle gives the effort, and your hand holds the load.

items.p: Why is your arm built so that the muscle must pull so hard?
opts: Your hand moves far and fast while the muscle shortens only a little
items.why: It's a trade-off. A small shortening of the muscle swings your hand a long way, fast. That lets you throw and catch. Picking 'a mistake' is a fair first guess. But nature trades strength for speed here.

items.p: Mountain roads up the ghats zigzag instead of going straight up. Why?
opts: A longer, gentler road needs a smaller push from the engine
Because straight roads are not allowed
items.why: A zigzag road is a long ramp. It is longer, but gentler, so trucks and buses can climb with less push. Picking 'shorter' is the opposite. Zigzags make the trip longer.
items.context: Ghats are hills and mountains in India, like the Western Ghats. Roads climbing them often zigzag back and forth.

items.p: A small child wants to lift a big brother on a see-saw. Give two different ways to make it work. Explain each one.
items.a: One way: the brother slides in closer to the middle, so his weight turns the plank less. Another way: two small children sit together at the far end, so there is more weight far out.
items.why: Moving weight further out, or adding more weight far out, both increase the turning.

items.p: A machine helped you push less. What did you have to give up? Give an example.
items.a: I had to push for a longer distance. For example, on a long ramp I pushed gently but for a long way.
items.why: Every machine trades a smaller push for a longer distance.

items.p: A ruler lever lifts a book. You press down on the far end. The pencil is the fulcrum. Show the forces on the ruler with arrows.
items.obj: a ruler on a pencil, lifting a book
items.why: You push down on one end. The book presses down on the other end. The pencil fulcrum pushes up and holds the ruler up. There is no sliding, so friction is not the main force here.

items.p: Design a ramp for a toy car to reach a 10 cm high box. Draw a short steep ramp and a long gentle ramp. Mark which needs the smaller push.
items.a: Two ramps from the floor to the top of the box. The long gentle ramp is marked as the smaller push.
items.why: The longer ramp to the same height needs a smaller push.
items.art: A box 10 cm high on a floor line.

items.p: Predict: 2 coins on left peg 3. 3 coins on right peg 2. What happens?
items.why: 2 times 3 is 6. 3 times 2 is 6. Both sides make 6, so it balances. Picking 'tips right' means counting coins and forgetting distance.
items.context: This is from the Balance Bazaar game. A ruler on a pencil is a see-saw. The pegs are numbered 1 to 4 going out from the middle.

items.p: A key on peg 4 balances 2 coins on peg 2. The key weighs the same as ____ coin.
items.why: 2 coins times 2 is 4. The key times 4 must also be 4. So the key weighs 1 coin. This is how you weigh an unknown thing with a lever.
items.context: This is a mystery card from the Balance Bazaar game. The pegs are numbered 1 to 4 going out from the middle of a ruler see-saw.

items.p: Why can't a wheel with shifting weights keep turning for ever by itself?
opts: It could, nobody has tried hard enough
The turning on both sides always balances out, and friction slowly stops it
items.why: Every design ever tried has failed. Energy cannot come from nothing. Picking 'nobody has tried hard enough' is a hopeful guess. In fact people have tried for over 800 years, since Bhaskara II described one in about 1150.
items.context: For hundreds of years, inventors dreamed of a wheel that turns for ever by itself, with no push.

items.p: The Earth is about 81 times heavier than the Moon. Where is their balance point?
opts: Much closer to the centre of the Earth, inside the Earth
items.why: Like a heavy grown-up near the middle of a see-saw, the heavy Earth is close to the balance point. It is about 4,700 km from the Earth's centre, inside the Earth. Picking 'halfway' means forgetting that the Earth is far heavier.

answer_chart.title: How far the Earth-Moon balance point is from the centre of the Earth

data.label: Earth's centre to the balance point

answer_chart.note: The balance point is inside the Earth, about 1,700 km below the surface.

items.context: The Earth and the Moon both swing round one shared balance point, like the two ends of a see-saw.

items.p: Astronomers can find planets round other stars by watching the stars wobble.
items.why: True. A planet and its star swing round a shared balance point, so the star wobbles a little. In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found a planet this way.

items.p: Inside your muscles, tiny molecules called myosin pull on threads. How do they make a small movement bigger?
opts: Each one has a stiff arm that swings like a lever
items.why: A myosin head grabs a thread, and its stiff neck swings like a lever, making a tiny change into a bigger step. Picking 'glue' is a sensible guess, because they do grab on. But they also let go and swing again.

items.p: Who should get credit for the lever?
opts: Only the person who first used it
The many unnamed people who used it, and Archimedes who explained its rule
items.why: Farmers used levers like the shaduf long before Archimedes. He was the first we know of to prove the rule. Picking 'only Archimedes' is what many books say, because his work was written down.

items.p: Put these in order from SMALLEST push needed to BIGGEST, to raise the same load 1 metre: lifting straight up, a 2 m ramp, a 4 m ramp, a 3 m ramp.
items.why: The longer the ramp to the same height, the smaller the push. Lifting straight up needs the biggest push.

items.p: A screw is a ramp wrapped round a rod. Why does a screw grip wood so strongly?
opts: Many turns of a small push move it in only a little, with a big force
items.why: A screw is a long ramp. Each turn moves it forward only a little, so a small twist gives a big push forward. Picking 'sharp' is part of it, since the tip is a wedge. But the thread is a ramp.

items.p: A see-saw has a child of 20 kg sitting 2 metres from the middle. Where must a 40 kg grown-up sit to balance?
opts: Half a metre from the middle
items.why: 20 times 2 is 40. The grown-up is 40 kg, and 40 times 1 is 40. So the grown-up sits 1 metre from the middle. Picking 4 metres means thinking the heavier person must go further out. It is the opposite.

items.p: The peoples of ancient Mexico made toys with wheels but did not build carts. Give two possible reasons.
items.a: They had no horses or oxen to pull carts. Their land had thick jungles and steep mountains, where carts would be hard to use. Perhaps people carrying loads, or canoes on lakes, worked better.
items.why: There is no single answer. Historians still debate it. A good answer gives reasons based on the land and animals.
items.context: Archaeologists have found little clay animal toys on wheels in Mexico, many centuries old. But the people there did not use wheels for carts.

items.p: Ramp guides in many countries, including India, suggest a ramp should be about 12 times as long as it is high, for wheelchairs. Why do you think it must be so long?
items.a: So the slope is gentle. Then a person in a wheelchair can push themselves up with a small push, and won't roll back down too fast.
items.why: A long, gentle ramp needs a smaller push. That matters for people who push with their arms.

items.p: Archimedes said, 'Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth.' Was he right? Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.a: For: the lever rule has no limit, so a long enough lever could make a tiny push into a huge one. Against: the lever would be impossibly long and stiff, there is nowhere to stand, and the push would take longer than the age of the universe.
items.why: There is no one right answer. A good answer uses the lever rule and also thinks about the real world.

items.p: Which machine changes the DIRECTION of a force, more than its size?
items.why: With a single pulley over a well, you pull down and the bucket goes up. The pull is about the same size. Picking the nutcracker means mixing up direction and size. A nutcracker makes your squeeze stronger.

items.p: A wheelbarrow carries a heavy load of bricks. Where are its fulcrum, load and effort? Why is it easier than carrying the bricks?
items.a: The fulcrum is the wheel. The load is the bricks in the middle. The effort is my hands lifting the handles. My hands are further from the wheel than the bricks, so I lift with a smaller force. The wheel also rolls instead of dragging.
items.why: A wheelbarrow is a lever with the load in the middle, and it has a wheel, so it uses two simple machines.

items.p: A see-saw is level. A 30 kg child sits on one side, and a 15 kg child sits on the other. Where could each one be sitting? Give one answer and explain it.
items.a: The 15 kg child sits twice as far from the middle as the 30 kg child. For example, the 30 kg child sits 1 metre from the middle and the 15 kg child sits 2 metres away. 30 times 1 is 30, and 15 times 2 is 30.
items.why: Any answer where the lighter child is twice as far out is right. A good answer shows that weight times distance is the same on both sides.

items.p: Draw your own design for a machine that lifts a bucket of water from a well, using at least two simple machines. Label each one.
items.a: Any design using two or more simple machines, labelled. For example: a lever like a shaduf with a stone counterweight, and a pulley wheel.
items.why: Real machines often combine simple machines.

experiments.title: The Ruler See-saw: can one coin beat two?
experiments.question: Can one coin balance two coins? If so, where must it sit?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put 2 coins on one side of the ruler. Where will 1 coin on the other side make it balance? Point to the place, and say why you think so, before you test.
experiments.fair_test: Use coins that all look exactly alike. Keep the pencil in the same place, under the middle of the ruler. Change only one thing at a time: the number of coins, or where they sit. Try each balance twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Coins times distance on each side

materials.item: a 30 cm ruler. A wooden or steel one is best, because a thin plastic one bends.
a round pencil
10 coins that all look exactly alike, such as 1-rupee coins of one design. Older and newer coins can weigh different amounts.
a small, thin book, and some sticky tape
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: No special safety needed. Keep coins away from very small children, who might swallow them.

schedule.what: Balance coins on a ruler see-saw. Find the rule. Fill in the table. Then lift a small book with the ruler.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then, for each row, multiply coins by distance on each side. What do you notice?

flow.do: 1. Lay the round pencil on a flat table. Stick each end down with a small piece of tape, so it cannot roll. 2. Lay the ruler across the pencil. 3. Slide the ruler until it balances with nothing on it. The pencil should be near the 15 cm mark.
flow.say: This ruler is a see-saw. The pencil is the fulcrum. The fulcrum is the point a lever turns on. Let's make it balance with nothing on it.
flow.kid: Put the ruler across a round pencil. Slide it until it balances. The pencil is the fulcrum.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ruler see-saw experiment. You balance coins on a ruler laid across a pencil, and find the rule for balancing.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 coin 6 cm to the left of the pencil. 2. Ask your child to balance it with 1 coin on the right.
flow.say: One coin on each side. Where does the second coin go?
flow.kid: Put 1 coin on the left, 6 cm from the pencil. Where does 1 coin on the right go? Try it.

ask.q: Why does it balance when both coins are 6 cm away?

flow.do: 1. Now put 2 coins in a pile, 6 cm to the left. 2. Your child guesses where 1 coin must go on the right, then tests. 3. Write the result in the table. 4. Try 3 coins at 4 cm on the left, balanced by 1 coin.
flow.say: Here's the big question. Can one coin balance two? Guess first, then slide it until the ruler is level.
flow.kid: Put 2 coins on the left, 6 cm away. Can 1 coin balance them? Slide it out slowly. Where does it balance? Write it down.
flow.parent: 2 coins at 6 cm balance 1 coin at about 12 cm. 3 coins at 4 cm also balance 1 coin at about 12 cm. Measure to the middle of each coin. The ruler rarely stays perfectly level. Slide the coin out slowly. At first the 2-coin side stays down. Then, at one spot, the ruler tips over to the 1-coin side. The balance point is just there. Real rulers and coins are not perfect, so a centimetre out is fine. Do not tell the rule yet. Let your child look for it.

flow.do: Help your child multiply coins by distance for each side, for every row of the table.
flow.say: Let's multiply. Coins times distance on the left. Then coins times distance on the right. What do you notice?
flow.kid: For each row, do coins times distance on the left. Then do the same on the right. What do you notice?

check.q: 2 coins sit 6 cm from the pencil. 1 coin balances them. How far away is it?
check.why: 12 cm is right: 2 coins times 6 cm is 12, and 1 coin times 12 cm is 12. Picking 6 cm means matching the place but forgetting the weight. Picking 3 cm means thinking fewer coins must sit closer in. It is the other way round.

chart.y: Coins times distance from the pencil
chart.note: Both sides make 12, so the ruler balances.

flow.do: Try the rule on a new one before testing: 4 coins at 3 cm on the left. Where do 2 coins go on the right?
flow.say: Now use the rule to predict. 4 coins at 3 cm. Where do 2 coins balance them? Work it out first, then test.
flow.kid: 4 coins at 3 cm. Where do 2 coins go? Work it out first. Then test it.
flow.think: Archimedes found this rule about 2,200 years ago. Could you have found it without the ruler and coins?

flow.do: 1. Put a small book on one end of the ruler. 2. Slide the ruler along until the pencil is about 3 cm from the book. 3. Your child pushes down the far end with one finger. 4. Slide the ruler back until the pencil is under its middle, and push again.
flow.say: Now let's lift something heavy with our lever. Where should the pencil be to make it easy? And how far does your finger have to go?
flow.kid: Put a small book on one end of the ruler. Slide the ruler so the pencil is close to the book. Push the far end down with one finger. Now slide the ruler so the pencil is in the middle. Which is easier?

ask.q: When the fulcrum was close to the book, what did your finger have to do?
good: Move a long way down, while the book went up a little.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me what you found out, in three parts. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: one coin can balance two coins if it is twice as far from the fulcrum. What I saw: 2 coins at 6 cm balanced 1 coin at 12 cm. Why: a weight further from the fulcrum turns the ruler more. 2 times 6 is 12, and 1 times 12 is 12, so the turning is the same on both sides.

experiments.title: The Ramp Test: long and gentle, or short and steep?
experiments.question: Does a longer ramp make it easier to pull a load up to the same height?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will it be easiest to lift the toy truck straight up, pull it up a short steep ramp, or pull it up a long gentle ramp? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the ramp's length. Use the same truck with the same load, and the same height of book pile. Pull slowly and steadily, the same way each time, along the line of the ramp. Measure how far the rubber band stretches while the truck is moving. Do each test 3 times.

materials.item: a toy truck or car with free-turning wheels, loaded as heavily as it can carry, up to about 500 grams, such as a packet of dal or salt taped on top. With no toy car, a packet dragged on a steel plate works too, but friction makes the differences smaller.
a pile of books about 10 cm high
two flat boards: one about 30 cm long, such as a chopping board or a tray, and one about 60 cm long, such as a strip cut from a big cardboard carton and folded double so it does not sag
a long thin rubber band and a piece of string
a ruler

experiments.safety: Keep the rubber band away from faces. Pull gently, so it does not snap.

schedule.what: Lift the truck straight up, then pull it up a short ramp and a long ramp. Measure the rubber band stretch each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each way. Also write how far the truck travelled each time.

flow.do: 1. Make a pile of books about 10 cm high. 2. Tie the string to the front of the truck. 3. Loop the other end of the string through the rubber band and tie it. 4. Hold the rubber band by its free end. 5. Measure the band before you pull, and write down its length.
flow.say: We'll use the rubber band to measure how hard we pull. A bigger pull stretches it further.
flow.kid: Tie string to the truck. Tie a rubber band to the string. Measure the band before you pull. A bigger pull stretches it more.
flow.parent: The stretch is how much longer the band gets when you pull. Take the length before pulling away from the length while pulling. Work as a pair: your child pulls, and you hold the ruler beside the band and read its length. If you have a forcemeter from the Measuring forces unit, use it instead, and read the pull in newtons. A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures pulls.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ramp test. You pull a loaded toy truck up to the top of a pile of books, in three different ways, and measure how hard you pull.

flow.do: 1. Lift the truck straight up by the rubber band, slowly, from the table to the top of the book pile. 2. While it is rising, measure the band's length with the ruler. 3. Take away the length before pulling. That is the stretch. Write it down. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: First, lift it straight up. How far does the band stretch?
flow.kid: Lift the truck straight up by the rubber band. Measure the band while it rises. Write the number down.

flow.do: 1. Lean the short board from the table up to the top of the books. 2. Pull the truck slowly up the ramp, and measure the band's length while the truck moves. 3. Do the same with the long board. 4. Test each one 3 times.
flow.say: Now the short, steep ramp. Then the long, gentle one. Which stretches the band less?
flow.kid: Lean the short board on the books. Pull the truck up slowly. Measure the band. Now try the long board.

ask.q: Which ramp made the band stretch least?

flow.parent: The long ramp should need the least pull. The difference can be small if the truck's wheels are stiff, because friction adds a little to every pull. If the band hardly stretches on the ramps, use a thinner band or a heavier load. If the results are muddled, add more weight to the truck. Lifting straight up should always stretch the band the most, by far.

flow.do: Measure how long each ramp is, and compare the distances the truck travelled.
flow.say: Here's the catch. The long ramp needed less pull. But how far did the truck go?
flow.kid: Measure each ramp. How far did the truck travel each time? Smaller pull, but longer way!

check.why: The truck had to travel further. A smaller pull always means a longer way. Picking 'nothing' means thinking machines are free. Picking 'lighter' mixes up the truck's weight with the pull needed.

flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. One bar for each way of lifting the truck.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each way. Make it as tall as the middle stretch. Which bar is shortest?
