experiments.title: The Well Winch: a wheel and axle on a small box
experiments.question: Does a bigger handle make it easier to wind up a load?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will it be easiest to wind up the bottle by turning a bare pencil, a small handle, or a big handle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep the load and the pencil the same. Change only the size of the handle you turn. Count how many turns it takes to lift the bottle 20 cm, and say how hard each one felt.
results_table: How hard it felt: easy, medium or hard
Turns to lift the bottle 20 cm
How far your hand travelled: short, medium or long

materials.item: a small, strong carton, such as a tea or biscuit box, at least 4 cm narrower than your pencil is long. A shoebox is usually too wide.
a round pencil
string, about 60 cm long
a small plastic bottle with about 300 ml of water in it, with the string tied round its neck
two strips of stiff cardboard about 2 cm wide, one 5 cm long and one 15 cm long, to make handles
tape, a pair of scissors and a heavy book

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the box with the point of a pair of scissors.

schedule.what: Build the winch. Lift the bottle by turning the bare pencil, then a small handle, then a big handle.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw your winch and label the wheel, or handle, and the axle.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes a hole in each long side of the box, near the top. Put both holes about 3 cm from one short end. 2. Push the pencil through both holes, so it can turn. Leave about 3 cm sticking out on one side. 3. Tape one end of the string to the middle of the pencil. 4. Put the box on a table, with that short end right at the table's edge. Put a heavy book in or on the far end of the box, so it cannot tip. 5. Run the string over the short end and down past the table's edge. 6. Tie the bottle to it.
flow.say: This is a model of a well winch. The pencil is the axle. Winding it will pull the bottle up, the way a real winch pulls up a bucket.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes two holes in the box. Push a pencil through. Tape string to the pencil. Hang the bottle over the table's edge.
flow.context: This is the first step of the well winch experiment. You build a model of the winding machine on a village well, from a small box and a pencil.

flow.do: 1. Turn the bare pencil with your fingertips to wind up the string. 2. Count the turns to lift the bottle 20 cm. 3. Notice how hard it is.
flow.say: Wind it up by twisting the bare pencil. How does it feel?
flow.kid: Twist the bare pencil with your fingers. Lift the bottle. Is it easy or hard? Count the turns.
flow.parent: Turning the bare pencil takes a firm grip, and fingers may slip. That is the point. If it feels easy, add more water to the bottle.

flow.do: 1. Tape the small card handle firmly to the end of the pencil that sticks out, so it points sideways like a crank. 2. Wind the bottle up by turning the handle's tip. 3. Then do the same with the big handle. 4. Count turns and note how hard each felt.
flow.say: Now a small handle, then a big one. Turn it from the very tip. What changes?
flow.kid: Tape the small handle on the pencil. Turn it by its tip. Now try the big handle. Which is easiest?

ask.q: Why is the big handle easiest?
good: My hand is further from the pencil.
My hand goes round a bigger circle with a small push.

flow.do: Compare how far your hand travelled with each handle, for the same lift.
flow.say: The bottle went up the same 20 cm each time. Did your hand travel the same distance?
flow.kid: The bottle went up 20 cm each time. With the big handle, did your hand travel further?

check.q: With the big handle, the winding was easier. What did your hand do?
options: It travelled round a bigger circle
check.why: Your hand went round a bigger circle. The big handle traded a small push for a long way. Picking 'a shorter way' is the opposite of what happens. Picking 'stayed still' means the turning was not noticed.

flow.think: A tap, a doorknob and a screwdriver handle all work like your winch. Can you find one at home?

flow.do: Tell your child about real well winches. Tell them about the rahat, or Persian wheel. It lifted water in India for centuries, with a chain of pots.
flow.say: Wells in many villages had winches like this, with a long handle. Big wheels turned by bullocks lifted pots of water for the fields.
flow.kid: Real wells had winches like yours. Some had giant wheels turned by bullocks!

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me what you found out, in three parts. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a bigger handle makes winding easier. What I saw: turning the bare pencil was hard, the small handle was medium and the big handle was easy. My hand went round a much bigger circle with the big handle. Why: my push was further from the axle, so a small push made a strong twist.

experiments.context: In this experiment you build a model well winch from a small box and a pencil. You find out whether a bigger handle makes it easier to lift a bottle of water.

activities.title: Lever Hunt: at home and in your body

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Do not touch knives, cookers or sharp tools. Point to them instead.

schedule.what: Find 10 simple machines at home and 3 levers in your body.

activities.record: Make a list of 10 machines. Write LEVER, RAMP or WHEEL beside each. For each lever, draw a dot where its fulcrum is.

flow.do: Explain the hunt and give your child the paper and pencil.
flow.say: We're machine detectives. Let's find 10 simple machines in our home, and 3 hidden in your own body.
flow.kid: You're a machine detective! Find 10 simple machines at home. Then find 3 levers in your body.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lever Hunt. Simple machines are tools that make pushes and pulls easier. Levers turn on a point called a fulcrum.

flow.do: Walk through the home together. Look in the kitchen, at doors and taps, in a toolbox and in the cupboard.
flow.say: Is this a lever, a ramp or a wheel? If it's a lever, where does it turn?
flow.kid: Look in the kitchen and at doors and taps. Is it a lever, a ramp or a wheel? Where does it turn?
flow.parent: Good finds: chimta tongs, a nutcracker or sarota, scissors, a bottle opener, a spoon opening a tin, a stapler, a nail clipper, a broom (levers). A doorknob, a tap handle and a screwdriver (wheels and axles). A rolling pin (a roller). A jar lid (a screw). A knife (a wedge). A ramp at the building entrance (an inclined plane).

ask.q: Where is the fulcrum of a pair of scissors?

flow.do: 1. Help your child find levers in their body. 2. Bend the elbow, stand on tiptoe, nod the head, and open and close the jaw.
flow.say: Your body is full of levers. Bend your arm. Where does it turn? Now go up on tiptoe. Now nod.
flow.kid: Bend your arm. Where does it turn? Stand on tiptoe. Nod your head. Open your jaw. Find each fulcrum.

check.q: When you bend your arm, what is the fulcrum?
check.why: Your elbow is the fulcrum, where the arm turns. Picking 'your muscle' mixes up the effort, the muscle's pull, with the fulcrum. Picking 'your hand' mixes up the load with the fulcrum.

flow.think: Your body was not designed by an engineer. So how did it end up full of levers?

activities.context: This is a hunt for simple machines around your home, and for levers in your own body.

activities.title: The Park See-saw: lift a grown-up

materials.item: a see-saw in a park or playground

activities.safety: A grown-up must be there. Hold the handles. Never put feet or hands under the see-saw. Get off slowly, warning the other person first.

schedule.what: Balance a grown-up on the park see-saw by moving along it.

activities.record: Draw where each person sat when the see-saw balanced. Write who was heavier.

flow.do: 1. The child sits at one end. 2. The grown-up sits at the very other end. 3. Notice what happens.
flow.say: Let's both sit at the very ends. What happens?
flow.kid: Sit at one end of the see-saw. A grown-up sits at the other end. What happens to you?
flow.context: This is the first step of the park see-saw activity. A see-saw is a lever with its fulcrum in the middle.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up slowly slides closer to the middle, a little at a time. 2. Stop when the see-saw balances, or the child can push the grown-up up.
flow.say: Now I'll slide closer to the middle. Tell me when you can push me up.
flow.kid: The grown-up slides closer to the middle. Can you push them up now? Tell them when to stop.
flow.parent: If the grown-up is twice as heavy as the child, the balance comes when the grown-up is about halfway to the middle. Slide slowly, and keep both feet ready to touch the ground.

check.q: To balance a light child, where should a heavy grown-up sit?
check.why: The heavy grown-up sits closer to the middle, so their weight turns the see-saw less. A child who picks 'at the very end' thinks the heavier person needs more room. That makes the tipping worse.

flow.do: Try other pairs, if there are other children. Then talk about how the see-saw is like the dhenki in the story, or the ruler see-saw.
flow.say: It's the same rule as our ruler and coins. Heavy close in, light far out.
flow.kid: Try with a friend. Who sits where? It's the same rule as the ruler and coins!
flow.think: Could two small children at one end lift a grown-up sitting at the other end? Where would everyone have to sit?

activities.context: If you have a park nearby: in this activity, a child lifts a grown-up on a park see-saw. They find that where you sit matters as much as how heavy you are.

materials.item: a computer or tablet with internet, to open the free PhET Balancing Act simulation

activities.safety: A grown-up opens the website. Take a break from the screen after 30 minutes.

schedule.what: Explore the Intro and Balance Lab screens, then play the Game screen, levels 1 to 4.

activities.record: For each game level, write your score. Write one new trick you learned at each level.

flow.do: 1. Open phet.colorado.edu and search for Balancing Act. 2. Open the Intro screen. 3. Put bricks on the plank, then remove the supports and watch.
flow.say: This is a free see-saw game made by scientists in America. Put some bricks on, then take the supports away. What happens?
flow.kid: Put bricks on the see-saw. Take the supports away. Does it tip? Try to make it balance.
flow.parent: Turn on the 'Level' and 'Rulers' options, so your child can see distances. The Intro and Balance Lab screens are for exploring. Let your child play freely before the game.
flow.context: This is the first step of the PhET Balancing Act activity. PhET is a free science website from the University of Colorado. Balancing Act is a see-saw game where you place bricks and people to make the plank balance.

flow.do: 1. Open the Game screen. 2. Play Level 1. 3. Then Levels 2, 3 and 4. 4. After each level, write the score and one new idea.
flow.say: Before each level, tell me your plan. Did you change your thinking?
flow.kid: Play Level 1. Write your score. Did you need a new idea? Then try Level 2, 3 and 4.

ask.q: What makes Level 2 harder than Level 1?
good: The weights are different, so I have to move them.
I have to think about distance as well as weight.

flow.parent: This step follows the founder's Balancing Act worksheet. At higher levels, the game asks for the mass of a mystery object, and to predict which way the plank will tip. The rule is mass times distance on each side.

flow.do: Try the mystery objects: use the game to find the mass of an unknown object.
flow.say: How can a see-saw tell you how heavy something is? Let's find the mystery mass.
flow.kid: Find the mystery object's weight. Balance it with bricks. How heavy is it?

check.q: A 10 kg brick balances a mystery object at the same distance on the other side. How heavy is the mystery object?
check.why: 10 kg. Things that balance at the same distance from the fulcrum weigh the same. Picking 20 kg or 5 kg would only be right if the mystery object sat at a different distance.

flow.think: How could a see-saw weigh something heavier than all your bricks put together?

activities.title: Body Levers: yoga and a water bottle

materials.item: a full water bottle
a yoga mat or a soft floor

activities.safety: Move slowly. Stop if anything hurts.

schedule.what: Feel the levers in your arm, foot and neck with slow movements.

activities.record: Draw your arm holding the bottle. Mark the fulcrum, the muscle and the load.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds a water bottle in one hand, arm bent at the elbow. 2. They put the other hand on the front of the upper arm. 3. They lift and lower the bottle slowly.
flow.say: Feel your muscle working. Where does your arm turn? Where does the muscle pull?
flow.kid: Hold a bottle. Put your other hand on your upper arm. Lift the bottle slowly. Feel the muscle. Where does your arm turn?

ask.q: Where does the muscle join your lower arm?

flow.context: This is the first step of Body Levers. Your bones are levers, your joints are fulcrums, and your muscles give the push.

flow.do: 1. Rise slowly onto tiptoe and down again, 5 times, like the yoga pose called tadasana on the toes. 2. Feel the calf muscle at the back of the lower leg.
flow.say: Your foot is a lever too. The ball of your foot is the fulcrum. Your calf muscle lifts your whole body.
flow.kid: Rise up on tiptoe. Go down slowly. Do it 5 times. Feel your calf at the back of your leg.

check.q: When you stand on tiptoe, where is the fulcrum?
options: The ball of your foot, under your toes
check.why: The ball of your foot, under your toes, is the fulcrum. Your body turns round it as you rise. Picking 'your heel' is common, because the heel moves. But the part that stays on the floor is the fulcrum.

flow.do: 1. Nod the head slowly, forward and back. 2. Feel the back of the neck. 3. Talk about how muscles at the back hold the head up like a see-saw.
flow.say: Your head sits on top of your spine like a see-saw. When you nod, which muscles hold it up?
flow.kid: Nod slowly. Feel the back of your neck. Your head is a see-saw on top of your spine!
flow.think: Inside your muscles are billions of tiny levers called myosin. Every movement you make is levers inside levers.

activities.context: In this activity you feel the levers in your own body: your arm, your foot and your neck.

activities.title: Find the Balance Point, then dance the Earth and the Moon

materials.item: a ruler, a broom and a hammer or a heavy-headed spoon
open space

activities.safety: Spin slowly, on a soft floor, and stop if you feel dizzy. Keep the hammer low.

schedule.what: Find the balance point of long things. Then spin round with a grown-up to act out the Earth and the Moon.

activities.record: Draw the broom with a dot at its balance point. Draw the Earth and the Moon with their balance point.

flow.do: 1. Balance a ruler on one finger. 2. Then balance a broom across two fingers, held apart. Slowly slide the fingers together until they meet. 3. Try a hammer or a big spoon.
flow.say: Where does the broom balance? Is it in the middle? Why not?
flow.kid: Balance a ruler on your finger. Now hold a broom on two fingers. Slide your fingers together slowly. Where do they meet?

ask.q: Why does the broom balance closer to its bristles?

flow.context: This is the first step of the balance point activity. Every object has one balance point, as if all its weight were there.

flow.do: 1. The child and a grown-up face each other, holding both hands, arms straight. 2. They spin slowly round together. 3. Notice who moves in the bigger circle.
flow.say: You're the Moon and I'm the Earth. We're on an invisible see-saw. Who moves in the bigger circle?
flow.kid: Hold hands with a grown-up. Spin slowly together. Who goes round the bigger circle? Who wobbles in a small circle?
flow.parent: The child moves round a big circle and the grown-up wobbles in a small one. They turn round a balance point nearer the heavier grown-up. The Earth and the Moon do exactly this. Their balance point is inside the Earth, about 1,700 km below the surface.

check.q: The Earth and the Moon swing round a balance point. Where is it?
check.why: Inside the Earth. The Earth is about 81 times heavier than the Moon, so the balance point sits close to the Earth's centre, about 1,700 km under the surface. Picking 'halfway' forgets that heavy things sit closer to the balance point, just like the grown-up on the see-saw.

flow.do: Talk about how astronomers find new planets by spotting stars that wobble.
flow.say: A planet makes its star wobble, just like you made me wobble. Astronomers watch for those wobbles to find planets round other stars.
flow.kid: A planet makes its star wobble, like you made the grown-up wobble. That's how we find planets round far stars!

flow.think: If you could see the Earth from far away, would you see it wobble once every month?

activities.title: The Door Test: where is it easiest to push?

materials.item: a door that swings easily
a paper cup with a string handle, and some coins
sticky tape and a ruler

activities.safety: Keep fingers away from the hinge side of the door. A grown-up holds the door still while setting up.

schedule.what: Push a door at different places. Then hang a cup of coins at different places to see where the door starts to swing.

activities.record: Write how many coins it took to start the door swinging at each place. Draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the door with one finger, close to the hinges. 2. Then in the middle. 3. Then right by the handle.
flow.say: Push with one finger near the hinges. Now in the middle. Now near the handle. Where is it easiest?
flow.kid: Push the door with one finger near the hinges. Then in the middle. Then by the handle. Which is easiest?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Door Test. A door is a lever that turns round its hinges. Here you find where a push turns it most easily.

flow.do: 1. Open the door halfway. 2. Put a chair a little way from the door, with its back facing the door. 3. Tape the string to the face of the door, 10 cm from the hinge. 4. Run the string straight out, at right angles to the door, over the chair back. Hang the cup from its end. 5. Add coins one at a time until the door starts to move. 6. Repeat at 40 cm and at 70 cm from the hinge.
flow.say: Let's measure it. How many coins does it take to make the door start to swing, near the hinge and far away?
flow.kid: Fix the cup's string to the door near the hinge. Add coins one by one. When does the door move? Now try far from the hinge.
flow.parent: A simpler way: just compare how hard one finger has to push. The cup method gives numbers for a chart. Doors with stiff hinges need more coins. If the door swings by itself, the floor is not level, so try another door. The pattern is what matters: far from the hinge needs far fewer coins.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many coins in a cup hung on a door it takes to make it start to swing
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Far from the hinge, a small force turns the door.

flow.do: Talk about why door handles are always far from the hinges.
flow.say: Why do you think every door handle is on the side away from the hinges?
flow.kid: Why are door handles always far from the hinges? Have you ever seen one near the hinges?

check.q: Why are door handles far from the hinges?
options: So the door is easy to turn with a small push
check.why: Handles are far from the hinges so a small push turns the door. Picking 'they look nice' misses the science. Try pushing near the hinges and feel how hard it is.

flow.think: A spanner with a long handle loosens a stuck nut more easily. Why?

projects.title: Build a Shaduf: the 4,000-year-old water lifter

materials.item: a long stick about 1 metre long, such as the handle of a floor mop or wiper, or a piece of bamboo, for the beam
a sturdy chair, whose back is the post
a small bucket or a plastic cup with a string handle
an old sock or a cloth bag filled with rice, dal or sand, for the counterweight
a bucket of water
string and sticky tape

projects.safety: Do this on a balcony, in a bathroom or outside, with a grown-up, because water will spill. Keep faces away from the swinging beam. Use small weights only.

schedule.what: Learn what a shaduf is. Build the post and tie the beam to it.
Add the cup and the counterweight. Find the best counterweight.
Lift water. Improve the design. Show the family how it works.

projects.record: Draw your shaduf and label the fulcrum, the load and the counterweight. Write how many cups of water you lifted in one minute, with and without the counterweight.

flow.do: Show your child a picture of a shaduf, or describe it. It is a long pole on a post. A bucket hangs from one end, and a heavy stone from the other.
flow.say: A shaduf is a lever for lifting water from a river or a well. Farmers used it about 4,000 years ago in Mesopotamia and Egypt. In India, a lever like it is called a picottah, or etram in Tamil.
flow.kid: A shaduf is a long pole on a post. A bucket hangs at one end. A heavy stone hangs at the other. Farmers used it 4,000 years ago!
flow.context: This is the first step of the shaduf project. A shaduf is an old water-lifting lever. Over three days, you build a small one and use it to lift water.

flow.do: 1. Use the top of a sturdy chair back as the post. 2. Tie the beam onto the top of the post, about one third of the way from one end. Tie it loosely, so it can rock. 3. Check it rocks up and down freely.
flow.say: This tie is the fulcrum. Where should it go? Let's try a third of the way along.
flow.kid: Make a post. Tie the long stick on top. It should rock like a see-saw. The tie is the fulcrum.

flow.do: 1. Hang the cup from the long end of the beam. 2. Dip it in the water. 3. Lift the full cup by pressing down on the short end with your hand. Notice how hard it is.
flow.say: Dip the cup in the water and lift it. How hard is it without a counterweight?
flow.kid: Hang the cup on the long end. Dip it in water. Press the short end down. Is it hard?
flow.wait: Come back to the shaduf tomorrow.

flow.do: 1. Hang the filled sock or bag on the short end. 2. Add or take out rice until a full cup of water rises almost by itself when you let go.
flow.say: The counterweight does the lifting. How heavy should it be? Too heavy, and you can't dip the cup. Too light, and it won't help.
flow.kid: Hang the filled sock on the short end. Add rice until a full cup lifts by itself.

check.q: The counterweight hangs on the short end, close to the fulcrum. How heavy must it be to lift a full cup on the long end?
options: Heavier than the full cup, because the short end is close to the fulcrum
Lighter than the full cup, because rice is lighter than water
It does not matter, because the post does all the lifting
check.why: The counterweight must be heavier than the full cup, because it sits close to the fulcrum. Close in, a weight turns the beam less, so it needs to be heavier. Picking 'the post does the lifting' mixes up the fulcrum with the effort.

flow.parent: The counterweight on the short end must be heavier than the full cup, because it is closer to the fulcrum. That is the see-saw rule. When it is right, you only pull down a little to dip the empty cup, and the counterweight lifts the full one.

flow.do: 1. Lift water for one minute, counting the cups. 2. Try once without the counterweight and once with it. 3. Ask your child to change one thing to improve it: the fulcrum place, the counterweight, or the cup.
flow.say: Let's be engineers. Change one thing and test again. Did it get better?
flow.kid: Count cups of water lifted in one minute. Then change one thing. Did it get better?

chart.title: Made-up example: cups of water lifted in one minute

flow.do: Your child shows the family how the shaduf works, naming the fulcrum, load and counterweight.
flow.say: Teach someone else. Who do you think first thought of this? Nobody wrote their name down.
flow.kid: Show your family your shaduf. Name its parts. Who do you think invented it?
flow.think: The first shaduf was invented by someone whose name nobody knows. Do you think they were a farmer, a child or a builder?

projects.context: In this 3-day project, you build a model shaduf. It is a lever with a bucket on one end and a heavy stone on the other, used for 4,000 years to lift water.

challenges.title: Lift the Rice Bag
challenges.problem: Raise a 1 kg bag of rice from the floor onto a chair seat, using the smallest pull you can. Measure your pull each time.
constraints: You may not lift the bag with your hands.
Use only things you find at home.
Measure your pull with a thick rubber band and a ruler, or a forcemeter. A thin band may snap under 1 kg.
materials: a 1 kg bag of rice in a cloth bag
a thick rubber band and string, or a forcemeter
boards, books, a mop or wiper handle and string
general: Make a ramp from a board, from the floor to the chair, and pull the bag up it.
Use a mop handle as a lever over a pile of books, with the bag near the fulcrum. It lifts the bag only a little way, so lift it in stages, adding a book under the bag each time.
Pass the string over the top of the chair back and pull down. Like a pulley, this changes the direction of your pull. Friction on the chair makes the pull a little bigger, not smaller.
creative: Put the bag on a strong toy truck and pull it up the ramp, so it rolls instead of sliding.
Use a shaduf-style counterweight on the other end of a lever.
Make a zigzag ramp, like a ghat road, from two boards.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, try it, and measure the pull. Is it better than the others? What did you have to give up?

flow.do: Hang the bag from a rubber band and lift it straight up, from the floor to the height of the chair seat. Measure how far the band stretches.
flow.say: First, let's measure how hard it is with no machine at all.
flow.kid: Lift the bag straight up by a rubber band. Measure how far the band stretches. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lift the Rice Bag. You measure how hard it is to lift a bag of rice straight up, before trying machines.

flow.do: Plan three ideas together before trying any.
flow.say: Engineers plan first. Which machines could help? Let's draw three ideas.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer! Draw three ideas. Use a lever, a ramp or a wheel.

flow.do: Try each idea one at a time, measuring the pull each time.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time. Measure the pull. Which works best?

flow.parent: 15 times 12 is 180 cm, which is 1 metre and 80 centimetres. Children are often surprised how long a good ramp must be.

quiz.p: What does a simple machine do?
opts: Makes a push or pull easier, by changing its size or direction
quiz.why: A simple machine makes a push or pull easier. A child who picks 'makes energy' thinks machines give out extra. They never do. Picking 'a motor' is common, but a see-saw has no motor.

quiz.p: Which of these is a machine?
opts: A spoon used to pry open a tin
A pebble lying on the ground
quiz.why: The spoon is a lever, so it is a machine. Picking a pebble or a puddle means not yet linking machines to helping a push or pull.

quiz.p: On a see-saw, what is the fulcrum?
opts: The post in the middle that it turns on
quiz.why: The fulcrum is where a lever turns. Picking 'the child' mixes up the load or effort with the fulcrum.

quiz.p: Which part of your body is a fulcrum when you bend your arm?
quiz.why: Your arm turns at the elbow. Picking 'your muscle' mixes up the effort, the muscle's pull, with the fulcrum.

quiz.p: A heavy grown-up and a light child want to balance a see-saw. What should they do?
opts: The grown-up sits closer to the middle
The child sits closer to the middle
quiz.why: Weight close to the fulcrum turns less. So the heavy grown-up moves in. Picking 'can't be done' means only weight is counted, not distance.

quiz.p: 2 coins sit 5 cm from the fulcrum of a ruler see-saw. Where does 1 coin balance them?
quiz.why: 2 times 5 is 10, and 1 times 10 is 10. Picking 5 cm means matching the place but forgetting the weight.

chart.title: Ruler see-saw: where one coin balances two coins (made-up example)
chart.y: Coins times distance from the pencil
chart.note: Both sides make 10, so the ruler balances.

quiz.context: A ruler laid across a round pencil makes a small see-saw. Coins are the weights.

quiz.p: You need to get a heavy box onto a high step. Which ramp needs the smallest push?
quiz.why: A longer, gentler ramp needs a smaller push, but over a longer way. A child who picks 'the same' thinks only the box's weight matters.

quiz.p: A longer ramp needs a smaller push. What is the catch?
opts: You must push it a longer way
quiz.why: Machines trade a smaller push for a longer distance. A child who picks 'no catch' thinks machines give something for nothing.

quiz.p: Why is a doorknob easier to turn than the thin metal rod inside it?
opts: The knob is a big wheel, so a small push makes a strong twist on the rod
quiz.why: A doorknob is a wheel and axle. Your hand goes round a bigger circle, with a smaller push. Picking 'softer' means comfort is mixed up with force.

quiz.p: Why is it easier to move a heavy box on rollers than to drag it?
opts: Rolling has much less rubbing than dragging
quiz.why: Rollers touch the floor at only a few spots that lift off as they turn, so there is much less friction. Picking 'lighter' mixes up weight with push.

quiz.p: In the ramp test, to make it fair, what should you change?
opts: The ramp and the truck's load
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change one thing only. Then you know that thing caused the difference. Picking two things means you can't tell which one mattered.
quiz.context: In the ramp test, you pull a loaded toy truck up to the same height on ramps of different lengths, and measure the pull with a rubber band.

quiz.p: Look at the chart from the ramp test. Which way needed the smallest pull?
quiz.why: The shortest bar is the long, gentle ramp, so it needed the smallest pull. Picking 'straight up' may mean the tallest bar was read as the best. Here a taller bar means more pull.

chart.title: Made-up example results: rubber band stretch when pulling a loaded toy truck up to the same height
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different. A longer stretch means a bigger pull.

quiz.context: In the ramp test, a rubber band shows how hard you pull. A longer stretch means a bigger pull.

quiz.p: Can any machine give out more work than you put in?
opts: No, a smaller push always means a longer way
quiz.why: Energy can't come from nothing. People have tried to build never-stopping wheels since at least 1150, and all failed. Picking 'a clever enough one' is a hopeful idea that no one has made work.

quiz.p: Where is the balance point of the Earth and the Moon?
quiz.why: The Earth is about 81 times heavier, so the balance point is close to it, about 1,700 km under the surface. Picking 'halfway' forgets that the heavier one sits closer to the balance point, just like on a see-saw.

quiz.p: Your biceps joins your arm close to the elbow. What does that give you?
opts: A hand that moves far and fast
quiz.why: With the muscle close to the fulcrum, a small shortening swings your hand far and fast. Picking 'a mistake' is a fair first guess, but it is a trade-off of strength for speed.

open_questions.q: Exactly how were the pyramids and other giant ancient buildings raised?
open_questions.why_open: Most experts agree ramps, levers and sledges were used. Which kinds of ramp, and how they were arranged, is still argued about, and new finds keep changing the picture.

open_questions.q: How did the builders of India's temples and stepwells, like those in Gujarat and Rajasthan, lift and place stones weighing many tonnes?
open_questions.why_open: Historians have good guesses: ramps, levers, rollers, ropes, pulleys and huge teams of workers. For most buildings, nobody wrote down exactly how it was done, or the names of the builders.

open_questions.q: Who first used a lever, a ramp or a wheel?
open_questions.why_open: It happened long before writing, and wooden tools rot away. The oldest wheels and toy carts we have found may not be the first.

open_questions.q: Why did the peoples of ancient Mexico use wheels on toys but not on carts?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas: no animals to pull carts, rough land, or other ways that worked better. Historians still debate it.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does each tiny myosin lever in a muscle time its swing?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can now see myosin's shape and watch single molecules move. The fine details of each step are still being studied.

open_questions.q: How small can a machine be?
open_questions.why_open: Chemists have built tiny motors, switches and even a 'nanocar' from single molecules. How useful such machines can become is still unknown.

open_questions.q: How many planets like the Earth are there round other stars?
open_questions.why_open: Stars' wobbles, and dips in their light, have revealed thousands of planets. Small, Earth-like planets make tiny wobbles that are very hard to see.

open_questions.q: Was the Thanjavur temple's capstone really hauled up a ramp several kilometres long?
open_questions.why_open: It is a well-known story, but there is no written record from the time it was built. Historians are still unsure.

maths.problem: On a ruler see-saw, 3 coins sit 4 cm from the pencil. How far away must 2 coins sit on the other side to balance them?
maths.explain: On the left, 3 coins times 4 cm is 12. On the right, 2 coins times something must also be 12. 2 times 6 is 12. So the 2 coins sit 6 cm from the pencil.
maths.context: A ruler laid across a round pencil makes a small see-saw. It balances when coins times distance is the same on both sides.

answer_chart.title: Both sides of the ruler see-saw

maths.why_maths: Multiplying coins by distance turns the see-saw rule into a sum, so you can find where a coin must go before you try it.

maths.problem: In the ramp test, suppose lifting the toy truck straight up 10 cm took 6 newtons on a forcemeter. Your long ramp was 60 cm long, reaching the same 10 cm high pile. With no friction, about how big would the pull up the long ramp be?
maths.explain: The ramp is 60 cm long and the pile is 10 cm high. 60 divided by 10 is 6, so the truck travels 6 times as far. Push times distance stays the same, so the pull is about 6 times smaller. 6 newtons divided by 6 is 1 newton. In real life friction adds a little, so you would measure a bit more.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying and sharing lets you predict how much a ramp will help before you build it, and then check your prediction with a forcemeter.
maths.context: In the ramp test, you pull a toy truck up to the top of a pile of books, straight up and then up ramps. A newton is the unit for measuring a push or a pull. A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures pulls in newtons.

maths.problem: A doorstep is 15 cm high. Ramp guides say a ramp should be 12 times as long as it is high. How long should the ramp be? Give your answer in metres and centimetres.
maths.answer: 180 cm, which is 1 metre and 80 centimetres.
maths.explain: 15 times 12: 15 times 10 is 150, and 15 times 2 is 30. 150 plus 30 is 180 cm. 100 cm make 1 metre, so 180 cm is 1 metre and 80 centimetres.
maths.context: This is from the challenge A Ramp for Everyone. A gentle ramp lets people in wheelchairs push themselves up with a small push.

answer_chart.title: Step height and ramp length (12 times as long)

maths.why_maths: Multiplying the step height by 12 tells you how long a ramp must be before anyone builds it, so it is gentle enough for a wheelchair.

maths.problem: Your biceps pulls 5 cm from your elbow. Your hand holds a water bottle 35 cm from your elbow. How many times as far from the elbow is your hand?
maths.explain: 35 divided by 5 is 7. Check: 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5 is 35. So the hand is 7 times as far from the fulcrum. That means the muscle must pull about 7 times as hard as the bottle's weight, and the hand moves 7 times as far.
maths.context: Your arm is a lever. Your elbow is the fulcrum, your biceps muscle pulls close to it, and your hand holds a load far from it.

chart.title: Your arm as a lever (typical grown-up numbers)
rows: Where your hand holds a load
How many times further the hand is

maths.why_maths: Dividing the two distances tells you how many times harder your muscle pulls, and how many times further your hand moves.

maths.problem: Think of the park see-saw. Suppose you weigh 20 kg and sit 2 metres from the middle. Your grown-up weighs 40 kg. How far from the middle must the grown-up sit to balance?
maths.explain: Child: 20 times 2 is 40. Grown-up: 40 times something must be 40. 40 times 1 is 40. So the grown-up sits 1 metre from the middle. The grown-up is twice as heavy, so sits half as far.
maths.context: A see-saw balances when weight times distance from the middle is the same on both sides.
maths.why_maths: A missing-number sum tells you where to sit on the see-saw without sliding back and forth guessing.

maths.problem: In the ramp test, the rubber band stretched 9 cm when the truck was lifted straight up, 4 cm on the short ramp and 2 cm on the long ramp. Draw a bar chart. How much less did it stretch on the long ramp than straight up?
maths.answer: 7 cm less. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each way, as tall as its stretch. Then 9 take away 2 is 7. So the band stretched 7 cm less on the long ramp.
maths.context: In the ramp test, a rubber band shows how hard you pull a toy truck up to the same height. A longer stretch means a bigger pull.

maths.why_maths: After the ramp test you have a list of numbers. A bar chart shows the easiest way at a glance, and subtracting shows how much the ramp helped.

roots.context: We have been learning how levers, inclined planes and wheels let a small push move a heavy load. Now we ask what that tells us about strength, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: On a see-saw, a light child can lift a heavy grown-up by sitting far from the fulcrum. The child is no stronger than before. She goes down a long way, and the grown-up rises only a little. So what a push can lift depends on where it is placed, not only on how hard it is.
deep_truth.habit: We think of strength as something inside a person, so the heavier or stronger one should always win. A lever shows that the same push can lift a little or a lot, depending on where it is placed.
deep_truth.evidence: In the ruler see-saw, one coin 12 cm from the pencil balanced two coins 6 cm from it. In the story, Jonaki lifted the dhenki's heavy head only when she stood at the very end of the beam.

three.who_am_i: Your arm is a lever, with your elbow as its fulcrum. Your muscle pulls close to the elbow, so your hand can move far and fast.
three.what_is_life: Every movement you make comes from billions of tiny myosin molecules swinging like levers inside your muscles.
three.what_is_this_world: No machine anywhere has ever given out more work than was put in. A smaller push always has to travel further.

roots.thread: A lever, an inclined plane, a wheel and axle, a pulley, a wedge and a screw look like six different tools. Underneath, they all make the same trade: a smaller force over a longer distance. The push times the distance stays the same, so nothing is made and nothing is lost. It is only shared out differently. Physics keeps finding this: things that look separate follow one rule underneath. Six machines sharing one rule is a small, clear example, and a child can test it with a ruler and some coins.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 3, the story of Cook Ding
teachings.teaching: A cook carves an ox so skilfully that his knife stays sharp for nineteen years. He never hacks at bone. He guides the blade through the natural gaps between the joints.
teachings.link: A knife is a wedge. Cook Ding puts it exactly where the joints already come apart, so a small push does the cutting. Like Jonaki at the end of the dhenki beam, where the force goes matters as much as how big it is.

teachings.teaching: The monk Nagasena asks King Milinda: is the chariot the wheels? The axle? The pole? No single part is the chariot. 'Chariot' is the name for all the parts put together.
teachings.link: A bicycle is levers, wheels and axles and a chain, working as one. 'Bicycle' is the name for all of them together. Your body is the same, with its bones, muscles and joints.

science.text: A machine can make a push smaller, but it never makes energy. A smaller push always has to travel further. Friction turns a little of the energy into heat.
Inside your muscles, tiny molecules called myosin swing like levers and pull thin threads past each other. That is how every muscle shortens.

other_view.who: René Descartes, a French philosopher of the 1600s
other_view.view: Descartes argued that animal bodies are machines: parts pushing parts, like a clock, with nothing more to them. Many scientists today also explain living bodies as very complex machines.

practice.title: Find your lever
practice.say: Let's hold one arm out in front, palm up. Slowly bend it at the elbow and bring your hand to your shoulder. Then lower it slowly. Do it three times, breathing out as you lift. Put your other hand on your upper arm and feel the muscle work. The muscle moves only a little, but your hand travels a long way. Your elbow is the fulcrum.
practice.kid: Bend your arm slowly at the elbow. Breathe out as you lift. Feel the muscle with your other hand. Your elbow is a fulcrum.

ask: Jonaki was no stronger at the end of the beam. So where did her extra lifting come from?
Are you a machine? What would make you more than one?
Is there anything in the world you get for nothing?
If no single part is the chariot, where is the chariot?

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, many inventors believed a clever machine could give out more than you put in. In about 1150, the Indian mathematician Bhaskara II described a wheel that carried mercury, a heavy liquid metal, sealed inside tubes. He thought it would turn for ever by itself. Inventors in Europe tried wheels like it for centuries. None of them worked. In 1586, a Flemish engineer called Simon Stevin used this failure to work out how ramps work. He imagined a loop of beads, like a necklace, hung over a triangle with one long, gentle slope and one short, steep slope. More beads lie on the long slope. Will they pull the loop round? If they did, the loop would keep turning for ever, and that never happens. So the loop must stay still. That means a few beads on a steep slope pull as hard as many beads on a gentle one. So a load needs a smaller pull up a longer, gentler slope. Stevin was so pleased that he put the picture of the beads on the title page of his book. In 1775, the French Academy of Sciences decided to stop checking machines that claimed to run for ever.
how_we_found_out.who: Simon Stevin, a Flemish engineer, after centuries of failed self-turning wheels
how_we_found_out.when: About 1150 to 1775, and Stevin's book in 1586
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many inventors believed a clever machine could give out more than you put in, and keep turning for ever. Stevin used the fact that this never happens to work out how ramps work.
